articles.title: Rand Fishkin’s Seattle game studio serves up first trailer for ‘The Snackbar at the End of the World’
articles.author: Kurt Schlosser
paras: If the eventual release of “The Snackbar at the End of the World” is a full-on meal for video game fans, news this week of the game’s first trailer should at least suffice as an appetizer.

Seattle-based Snackbar Studio , co-founded by SparkToro founder Rand Fishkin and his wife, writer Geraldine DeRuiter , unveiled its debut title and Steam page on Tuesday. The hand-drawn narrative adventure RPG puts players in the role of a chef trying to save a struggling family restaurant in a magical version of 1960s Italy.

The studio now plans to launch the game late next year, after originally targeting the second half of 2026. Snackbar raised $2.15 million from 38 angel investors two years ago, and the project began four years ago, according to Fishkin. The team includes five co-founders (Fishkin, DeRuiter, game designer Nicolas Kraj, lead programmer Miriam Cabrera and art director Francesco Mazza) plus about 10 contractors.

In the studio’s description on Steam, players forage for ingredients in the “forbidden wilds” outside town, battling explosive tomatoes, chaotic zucchini and vendetta-driven poultry. They then cook dishes back at the restaurant before a tyrannical mayor known as the Sindaco can shut it down. The game mixes combat and stealth with cooking mini-games based on real-world recipes.

The trailer is set to “’O surdato ’nnammurato,” a classic Neapolitan song performed by professional musicians recruited by the studio’s music director. Fishkin said he and DeRuiter both cried the first time they heard it.

Fishkin is best known in Seattle tech circles as co-founder of SEO software company Moz and audience research startup SparkToro, and he more recently launched Alertmouse, a tool for tracking online mentions. DeRuiter, a writer and author, is Snackbar’s head writer.

In a LinkedIn post this week, Fishkin recalled telling DeRuiter during the COVID lockdown that he wanted to fulfill a childhood dream of making a video game. Her reply: “Don’t wait. Do it now. I’ll do it with you.”

In the same post, he said the game’s themes include found family and fighting fascism “even when there’s no hope you’ll win.” He called it a love letter to DeRuiter’s small family village in the mountains outside Naples, to that era of Italy, to video games, and to the many people both of their families have lost in recent years.

Moments like hearing that song come often in the work, Fishkin said, such as when a new feature clicks or a new animation brings DeRuiter’s characters to life. He has always loved art without being good at any form of it. “I may not be able to create art, but I can enable it,” he said. “What a wonderful feeling.”

There have been lows, too. The team spent its initial 18 months on the project with a contract agency that didn’t work out, losing money with nothing to show for it. Fishkin is glad they kept going, “even when it felt financially irresponsible.”

The game is entirely human-made, and Snackbar’s no-AI stance is firm. “Geraldine hates AI with the fury of a thousand suns,” Fishkin said. He once suggested, just once, that she use Google’s AI Mode to find a synonym, and she was mad at him for the rest of a six-hour flight home from Philadelphia. Even if players, the rest of the team and the games media were fine with AI (and they’re not), DeRuiter alone would make it a no-go, he said.

Still ahead are 10 to 12 months of finishing the game’s content, playtesting, bug fixing, marketing and launch prep. Fishkin called it daunting, but said team members have done it many times before, “even though it’s our first rodeo.”

Fishkin is still juggling Snackbar with SparkToro and Alertmouse, and describes his role at the studio as mostly oversight and management. SparkToro is growing again, and Alertmouse recently hit a big milestone in annual renewals with high retention. He and his Alertmouse co-founders are putting more money into the company to fund growth.
Balancing the three roles is a challenge, he said, but only rarely completely overwhelming. “Like this week.”

articles.title: AWS gives developers a free local stand-in for its cloud, built from scratch by AI agents
articles.author: Todd Bishop
paras: AWS says its engineers didn’t write or review a single line of code in its newest developer tool, and the company is touting that as a selling point.

AWS Emulator, released Wednesday, simulates AWS services on a developer’s own machine. It’s built from more than 400 API models covering more than 200 AWS services. Developers and AI coding agents can use it to test code without a network connection and without paying for the real cloud.

The tool addresses a problem that coding agents such as Amazon’s Kiro and Anthropic’s Claude Code have made worse. Agents can write code faster than teams can test it against the real cloud. Agents check their work by running the code and reading the results, over and over, and doing that in the cloud adds delays and costs.
The emulator lets them run that loop on a developer’s own machine.
In an ironic or perhaps appropriate twist, AWS used AI agents to build the emulator. Agents also maintain it, testing it against real AWS and fixing the gaps they find.

“The emulator was written entirely by autonomous agents. Our team hasn’t written or reviewed any of the code,” wrote Matt Goldberg, the AWS senior principal engineer behind the project, in a blog post .

Goldberg compared his agents to himself as a kindergartner, too young to hold a crayon properly, who got yelled at by classmates for ruining a group drawing of dinosaurs. The problem wasn’t bad intent, he wrote, just a lack of competence. The answer, for agents, is clearly defined areas to fill in.
“I think agents also need coloring books,” he wrote.
The agents work from AWS’s public API models, which describe how each service should behave, and check their work against the real AWS cloud.

The agents run on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore in three teams. One writes “fidelity tests” — real-world scenarios such as creating a queue, sending a message and deleting the queue — and checks each against real AWS. A second runs those tests against the emulator and files issues for failures, and a third fixes them, one agent per issue.
Every change passes through an automated gate where other agents check coding standards and security. Goldberg wrote that hundreds of agents now fix thousands of issues a day.

The project started as a weekend experiment, inspired by Anthropic’s demonstration earlier this year in which a team of Claude agents built a C compiler . Goldberg gave Kiro a three-step prompt and got a passable first version of Amazon SQS, AWS’s message queuing service, in 15 minutes.
By the end of the weekend, Goldberg wrote, Kiro had built a rough version of the rest of AWS, with obvious gaps, and his team started using it to test its software that Monday.

Swami Sivasubramanian, AWS vice president of agentic AI and emerging tech, tied the project to a lesson he described to GeekWire in June. He spent four nights babysitting Kiro as it tried to rebuild a replication engine he and Allan Vermeulen built by hand nearly 20 years ago.
Once he gave the agent a spec and a way to test its work, the job took about two hours.

“When agents write the code and check their own work, the engineer’s job is to give them room to work on their own and to build the specs, tests, and merge gates that decide when that work is correct,” Sivasubramanian wrote in a guest post on CTO Werner Vogels’ blog.
It’s the same idea behind Amazon’s recent move to rewrite its engineering playbook for an era when AI writes the code.

The emulator has limits. Devin Pratt, an IDC analyst, told InfoWorld that it doesn’t yet simulate throttling, outages or differences in which services and features are available by region, and that it doesn’t sandbox the code it runs. The agents’ backlog of known gaps is public, in a GitHub folder called “things-that-do-not-work.”

Other AWS emulators exist, most notably LocalStack, which this year put its free version behind an account requirement and limited it to noncommercial use. AWS released its emulator for free under CC0, a public domain dedication, with the full commit history on GitHub.
The company says it will share more at its upcoming re:Invent conference.

articles.title: Tech Moves: Wizards of the Coasts names president; new execs at Skydance, Pulumi, Marchex and Syndio
articles.author: Lisa Stiffler
paras: — Dan Ayoub , the past head of Dungeons & Dragons, has been named president of Wizards of the Coast & Hasbro Digital Games . Ayoub joined the Renton, Wash.-based Wizards of the Coast in 2022 and counts himself among the longtime players of D&D and Magic: The Gathering.

“D&D is 52 years old. Magic is 33. Brands don’t last that long because of any one leader; they last because generations of creators and fans keep choosing them,” Ayoub said . “We owe it to them to protect what makes these worlds special.”
Earlier in his career, Ayoub spent more than a decade at Microsoft, primarily with its 343 Industries video game studio, now called Halo Studios.

— Farah Ali has joined the media company Skydance as vice president of engineering, based at its Bellevue, Wash., office. She previously spent a decade at Electronic Arts over two stints, most recently as vice president of AI transformation and technology.

Ali has also served as an affiliate professor at the University of Washington, teaching courses in software entrepreneurship, and as a technical advisor for Madrona Venture Labs. She was co-founder and chief technology officer of FreightWeb, a Seattle-based logistics technology startup.

Paramount Skydance last month completed its acquisition of Warner Bros. Discovery (WBD), with the combined company taking the name Skydance. Shortly after, the company announced the departure of two WBD leaders from the Bellevue site: Avi Saxena and Tyler Whitworth .
— Irene Chang has joined Pulumi as chief revenue officer. The Seattle startup automates cloud infrastructure tasks such as managing networks and databases, optimizing costs and ensuring compliance.

Chang said Pulumi’s culture and product won her over. “We automate deployments so teams can provision resources in seconds and scale from simple apps to enterprise architectures without losing control or compliance,” she wrote on LinkedIn.
Chang was previously Postman’s VP of corporate sales for the Americas and before that held VP roles at Cloudflare.
Pulumi is No. 15 on the GeekWire 200 , a ranked index of the Pacific Northwest’s top startups.

— Marchex , the Seattle-based, publicly traded call and conversation analytics company, has named Travis Fairchild as president. The news was disclosed in an SEC filing . Fairchild was previously with Marchex for 18 years in strategy and business development roles.
He left in 2021 to become CEO of Archenia, a Las Vegas-based customer qualification and acquisition company, which Marchex acquired in July.
Troy Hartless , who in September 2025 added president to his role as chief revenue officer, will return to serving solely as CRO.

— General Fusion has named David Janashvili as chief financial officer, effective Nov. 30. The Vancouver, B.C.-based company is developing fusion energy devices and became the first fusion venture to go public , through a SPAC. It trades on Nasdaq as GFUZ.

Janashvili joins from Surami Partners, which provides financial services for clean tech companies, and previously led climate tech investment banking at CIBC Capital Markets. Across numerous roles, he has advised boards and management teams of public and soon-to-be public companies.
— Gravity Payments has appointed CEO Tammi Kroll as chairman of its board of directors while she continues to lead the digital payments company.

“Her appointment as Chairman recognizes more than a decade of leadership at Gravity and her role in helping the company grow while remaining focused on the independent businesses and employees it serves,” the company said.

Kroll joined the company in 2015 as CTO, chief operating officer and chief information officer. She took over as CEO in 2022 after founder Dan Price resigned while facing assault and reckless driving charges. That case and a second were dropped, and Price maintained his innocence.
— Syndio , a Seattle-based pay equity startup, has two more leadership changes following the addition of seven new executives in April:
Syndio is No. 45 on the GeekWire 200 , a ranked index of the Pacific Northwest’s top startups.

— Seattle-based real estate brokerage Redfin has named Andy Swanton as general manager of rentals. He returns to the company after a short stint in 2022 as VP of properties. Swanton has also worked for Opendoor and BYD.

— Seattle cybersecurity company ExtraHop has appointed Rupert Clayson as head of sales for Europe, the Middle East and Africa (EMEA). The company reports growth in sectors including financial services and energy, and offers defense against AI-assisted security attacks. Clayson, who is based in London, joined from TeamViewer and was previously with Fortinet.

— POSaBIT Systems , a Seattle-based company providing point-of-sale and payments technology for the cannabis industry, has named Emily Eagon as CFO. Eagon joined POSaBIT last year as vice president of finance and has more than 25 years of experience in finance and accounting roles, including leadership at Verdigris and predictis.

— Benjamin Mullins has returned to Amazon as head of program management for the Devices Brand Studio. Mullins spent four years with Prime until 2019, when he left for a role at Oracle. He then joined Meta, where he was head of product for Reality Labs.

— Debra Bouchegnies has announced she is retiring from the University of Washington’s CoMotion Labs at the end of the year. Bouchegnies is CoMotion’s associate director of marketing and has been with the program since 2018. A replacement has not been named.
— Aman Dhingra has been appointed to the Technology Alliance board of directors. Dhingra has been with McKinsey & Co. for 17 years and serves as a partner.

articles.title: Seattle VC firm Ascend closes $17M fund to back ‘Third Act’ startups in physical AI and hardware
articles.author: Todd Bishop
paras: Venture firm Ascend has closed a $17 million third fund and landed its first institutional investor, in what founder Kirby Winfield calls the toughest fundraising market for small venture firms in 15 years.

The Seattle-based firm invests at the earliest stage, often writing the first check into a startup. It was the first investor in Overland AI , the maker of autonomous military vehicles, and an early backer of subsea geothermal startup Endurance Energy , among others.

Ascend Fund III will back more physical AI startups building robots, energy systems, defense technology and other ventures that blend software and hardware — part of a larger bet on what the Ascend team likes to call Seattle’s “Third Act.”

Winfield said raising a third fund in this market shows that Ascend has “arrived on the national stage,” along with Seattle’s rise as a hub for this new class of startups. He said the firm’s track record puts it in the same league as the country’s top seed investors.

“We are not just some nice guys in the corner of the country helping out our neighbors,” said Winfield, who works closely with Jen Haller , Ascend partner and chief of staff, and Nate Bek , a principal at the firm.

Who’s backing the fund: The new institutional investor is FirstLook Partners, a firm that invests in smaller venture funds. Josh Porter , FirstLook’s co-founder and managing partner, said the firm, which is “very bullish on the Seattle ecosystem,” looked at several startup markets outside San Francisco and New York and met many investors in Seattle, “but all roads kept leading back to Kirby.”
Porter said Winfield has “lived the founder journey” and has “the operational chops to sit across the table from a founder and empathize with what they’re going through.”
The rest of the fund comes from family offices, founders who have sold companies, and more than a dozen founders of Ascend portfolio companies.

A tough market for small funds: Ascend’s raise comes as smaller venture firms struggle to bring in new money. Their investors, mostly wealthy individuals and family offices, are waiting longer for returns from earlier funds.

Just 211 newer venture firms closed at least one fund through the end of September, down from 927 in all of 2022, according to the PitchBook-NVCA Venture Monitor . Established firms took a record 88.2% of the money raised by U.S. venture funds in the first nine months of the year, the report found. Porter said smaller firms have to show “a right to exist and a right to win deals.”

Ascend launched its first fund in 2019 and ultimately raised $15 million. Its second fund closed at $25 million in 2023. The firm generally operates in the $15 million to $25 million range and writes the same size checks regardless of fund size, Winfield said.
“We think Kirby knows his place in the larger ecosystem, knows the value he brings to the table, and has sized his fund accordingly,” Porter said.

The firm has already drawn about 60% of the money committed to Fund III. GeekWire first reported that the firm was raising the fund in April 2025, based on filings at the time. Endurance was one of the firm’s first investments from the new fund, in mid-2025 .

Ascend’s track record: Winfield started Ascend after two decades in leadership roles at four startups. He described the first fund as a proof of concept that “stumbled into some unicorns,” including Fabric, an e-commerce software company that was valued at $1.5 billion in 2022. Ascend was in its first round.

With its second fund, Ascend moved away from consumer and marketplace investing to focus on enterprise AI and deep tech. Its most successful investments from that fund, according to Winfield, include Overland AI, Sabi, Yoodli and Zocks.

After Ascend’s first checks, its portfolio companies have gone on to raise more than $1.5 billion from investors including Accel, Benchmark, Bessemer, Founders Fund, Khosla and Lightspeed, according to Ascend.

Ascend’s second and third funds rank in the top 10% of funds of $50 million or less, based on current valuations of their portfolio companies, Winfield said, citing figures Ascend shared with its investors at its annual meeting. The firm didn’t disclose specific returns or how much cash it has returned to its investors.

What Ascend looks for: The firm looks for ideas that seem too difficult, too boring, too confusing or too small for big multistage venture firms to evaluate. Ideally, Winfield said, its founders are doing something that makes Series A investors “a little bit nervous.”
That’s why Ascend hasn’t made many more defense tech investments since backing Overland, he said. Valuations for well-known founders in the sector have soared as more investors have piled in.
“The time to invest in defense tech was when nobody was investing in defense tech,” Winfield said.

Porter said Ascend’s focus on Seattle and physical AI is “really the bet we made with Ascend,” adding that Endurance and Overland have the potential to become “generational, category-defining companies.”
Fund III also backs AI software and infrastructure companies, including Seattle-area startup Govstream.ai, which uses AI to speed city permitting.

Seattle’s economic climate: Winfield is a champion of Seattle’s startup scene, known for Ascend’s annual Founders Bash party in the city and his ever-present ☔🔥☔ emojis on social media , symbolizing hot startups in rainy Seattle.

Ascend’s refreshed website and brand, launched with Fund III, nod to the firm’s Seattle roots with its longstanding Seattle Startup Toolkit and a Spotify playlist of Pacific Northwest indie rock and hip-hop.

But Winfield has also been a vocal critic of state and local policies he sees as hostile to startups, including Washington’s new tax on income over $1 million, which takes effect in 2028 and survived a repeal vote last week. He worries the tax could eventually be extended to people earning $150,000 a year, which would make it harder for startups to recruit employees from places like Texas.
“The chilling effect that’s going to have on the ecosystem is real, and it’s happening,” he said.
About 60% of Ascend’s portfolio companies are based in Seattle, according to the firm.

Bek said hardware companies such as Endurance and Overland still have good reasons to be in Seattle, including testing on Lake Union and in Yakima, access to the sea and University of Washington talent. For Overland, he said, that also means proximity to Joint Base Lewis-McChord.

Combined with the region’s history in aerospace, defense and energy, Winfield noted, those advantages make Seattle one of the country’s key hubs for building physical products. He called it “El Segundo Northwest,” a reference to the Los Angeles-area city that has become a hub for defense and hardware startups.

As Winfield notes, Ascend isn’t the only early-stage firm chasing these companies. Pre-seed firms such as Cantos, Ironspring and Silent Ventures are backing similar founders, and some Seattle firms that historically focused on software are becoming more open to investing in hardware.

Ultimately, he said, Seattle still benefits from a long legacy of technical founders, and Ascend is “betting that those folks are going to continue to create companies that are worth hundreds of billions of dollars.”

articles.title: Wilson Greenlights Expansion of Surveillance in Seattle
articles.author: Amy Sundberg
paras: On Tuesday, Seattle Mayor Katie Wilson announced that the City will be immediately moving forward with the expansion of the Seattle Police Department’s (SPD’s) surveillance program that was approved by city council last fall.

To assist her in this decision, Wilson engaged the New York University (NYU) Policing Project to perform a governance audit assessing the civil rights and liberties risks posed by SPD’s surveillance program, including their real-time crime center, CCTV cameras, and Seattle Department of Transportation (SDOT) cameras. Wilson said the City plans to implement many of the recommendations outlined in the report.
NYU didn’t assess the civil liberties risks of Seattle’s automated license plate readers due to their usage being suspended earlier in the year to comply with a new state law .

During her campaign, Wilson ran on an anti-surveillance platform, and at the beginning of her term, activists asked her to turn off all of SPD’s surveillance cameras. Instead, Wilson opted to postpone the installation of new SPD cameras in two new areas: the Capitol Hill nightlife district and an area around Garfield High School in the Central District. Wilson allowed new cameras to be installed in the Stadium District but only turned them on while Seattle was hosting World Cup matches this summer.
The NYU audit appears to have satisfied any qualms Wilson had about increasing the surveillance apparatus in Seattle.

“When I paused the expansion of CCTV, I did so because I believed we needed to ask some hard questions about data security and the protection of civil liberties, especially in the context of a federal administration that is targeting vulnerable communities and violating civil rights,” said Wilson. “After reviewing the evidence, the recommendations, and the safeguards available to us, I believe there is an important and responsible role for the RTCC within Seattle's public-safety system.”
The NYU Policing Project did not conduct any analysis around the cybersecurity risks of the data being collected by SPD.

Wilson said that Seattle has fewer surveillance cameras (so far) than many other American cities, an observation that hits differently at a time when the U.S. government is ramping up mass surveillance and the U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) is planning to deploy a domestic surveillance program in Seattle early next year.

Nevertheless, the surveillance cameras in the Stadium District will be turned back on immediately, and the City will proceed with the plans to procure and install cameras in the Capitol Hill nightlife district and the Central District.

“I also want to emphasize that these are not Flock cameras,” Wilson said. “Our system is managed by a company called Axon, and while there are obviously similarities in the technology, I think it's fair to say that Axon has a more responsive record.”

While less widely criticized than Flock, Axon has been receiving plenty of negative attention in its own right. In 2025 alone, Axon held $31.9 million in contracts with the U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE). And just last week, a class action lawsuit was brought against Axon, alleging that Axon “blatantly violated” rules enacted by the California State Legislature regarding how Axon can capture, use, and store the data collected by their license plate readers.

“Like its competitors, Axon sells a centralized, vendor-controlled camera system that municipalities rent,” said Noah Williams, a local cybersecurity expert and member of advocacy group Communities Not Cameras. “Unlike Flock, it provides municipalities with a false sense of control over their camera footage.”

Wilson’s change of heart came in spite of the NYU audit clearly stating that SPD’s real-time crime center does involve real civil liberties risks. “Short of ceasing to retain RTCC data altogether, SPD cannot eliminate fully the risk that such data could be obtained and used for purposes prohibited under Washington law,” the report reads.
Vulnerabilities include data obtained via public disclosure laws, data obtained via subpoena of either the City or Axon, and data obtained illegally.

The City of Seattle paid the NYU Policing Project $223,000 for the audit, which found the same kind of sloppiness, lack of clear policies, and failure to live up to commitments in SPD’s surveillance program that were highlighted in the recent audits by the Seattle Office of the Auditor and the other from the Office of the Inspector General (OIG).

The original SPD surveillance pilot installed cameras in the Third Street corridor downtown, the Chinatown-International District (CID), and Aurora Avenue in North Seattle. Since that time, SPD has been given access to a large number of SDOT traffic safety cameras through their real-time crime center, as well as incorporating 23 private cameras from three private businesses, all of which are located in the Capitol Hill nightlife district where Wilson had said she was pausing SPD camera surveillance.
The private cameras in Capitol Hill were plugged into SPD’s real-time crime center with no notice to community members.

Ryan Talen, a nurse who lives in Capitol Hill and member of Communities Not Cameras, was unaware of the private cameras in his neighborhood being streamed into SPD’s real-time crime center until The Urbanist let him know after the press conference.
“It's a violation of our privacy,” Talen told The Urbanist .

The University of Pennsylvania is performing a separate audit in cooperation with the OIG, initiated during Mayor Bruce Harrell’s term, on the efficacy of SPD’s surveillance program. According to the NYU audit, the University of Pennsylvania’s audit won’t be completed until late next year.
Not everyone found the NYU audit as reassuring as Wilson.

“The report revealed what we've known since visiting the RTCC,” Communities Not Cameras said in a statement. “The recommendations to reform the RTCC in the report are half-measures. More oversight, audit policies and targeted use won't eliminate the fact that this system can and will be abused. Seattle has had a long history of police brutality and corruption and a short history of community healing. We need more of the latter. Addressing poverty, mental health and solving root causes of crime is what will make us safer.”

The NYU audit was conducted by a team of lawyers who found that there are “significant gaps” in the governance around the real-time crime center and made 19 recommendations that the authors say should be implemented if SPD continues their surveillance program.

The audit’s purpose was not to call out the general benefits and risks of SPD’s use of the real-time crime center, nor to make a recommendation on whether SPD’s surveillance should continue as designed.

However, in an apparent contradiction to Wilson’s claims that adding more surveillance cameras to SPD’s real-time crime center will make Seattle “safer,” the audit states, “Although the potential benefits of the RTCC as described by the City are plausible, the current research base supporting these benefits is thin. There is more robust research studying the public safety impacts of CCTVs on their own (i.e., not connected to an RTCC), but that research is best characterized as mixed.”

At the press conference, Wilson appeared to be focused more on the potential upsides of surveillance, albeit not currently backed by empirical studies, as opposed to the costs of expanding a technology that is known to aid in repression and authoritarian control.
“Once data exists, no city or agency can guarantee it will never be shared,” the audit emphasized.

According to the audit, there is an important distinction between targeted surveillance and what a real-time crime center does, which is categorized as “indiscriminate surveillance,” meaning the system surveils the public at large and collects information about people who are not suspected of any offense or wrongdoing. Indeed, due to the real-time crime center integrating many different technologies, the audit says, “The centralization of surveillance systems and data can enable far more powerful and intrusive forms of surveillance than any one system could accomplish on its own.”

When considering the many gaps, lack of clear policy, and lack of follow-through outlined in the audit, it’s striking that SPD had an entire two years since council approval of the real-time crime center surveillance pilot to make progress on these goals. The real-time crime center became operational on May 20, 2025 . Thus, the City has been operating this surveillance system for almost a year and a half without the development of basic policies for its use and the timely delivery of commitments SPD made as part of the City’s Surveillance Impact Review process. This lack of engaging seriously with the agreements and responsibilities around using such a robust surveillance apparatus seems in line with SPD’s past conduct regarding surveillance technologies in the City.

Auditors found that there is a lack of clarity around the approved purpose of SPD’s real-time crime center, centering on whether it should be used for low-level misdemeanors as well as more serious incidents. According to the report, SPD found guidance that limited surveillance use for misdemeanors “challenging from an operational perspective,” and yet the surveillance pilot was originally passed with the intention of reducing gun violence and human trafficking (despite no empirical evidence has proven that this kind of surveillance reduces either of these categories of crime).

In practice, the City is left with a surveillance system that could theoretically be used to police low-level issues like trespassing, public drug use, or shoplifting a package of diapers. Wilson refused to comment on this possibility other than to state that she’s looking forward to the University of Pennsylvania report that she expects to provide information as to how the real-time crime center is being used. Wilson’s answer suggests that the Mayor’s Office doesn’t expect to fully understand how SPD is using its surveillance system until two and a half years after it went operational.

While “real-time” is in the name, in practice the crime center is also used after the fact to investigate past events. If surveillance footage were to be used by SPD after the fact to track someone without a warrant, this usage would raise constitutional concerns and could potentially land the City in legal hot water. However, Wilson said SPD does not currently use the center for this purpose.

In addition, there are no firm policies in place for how to use the real-time crime center for large events. While passive monitoring of SPD camera feeds appears to be prohibited by policy, in practice, the auditors discovered that SPD created a case number for the entire World Cup and streamed live camera feeds through the real-time crime center throughout World Cup events.

Surveillance at protests is another gray area of SPD’s surveillance program, and the audit recommends SPD develop policies around the real-time crime center and protest activities that are protected by the First Amendment. Currently, demonstrations are captured by default if they take place where SPD and SDOT cameras are installed.

In order to improve transparency, the audit recommended that SPD fulfill its two outstanding Surveillance Impact Review commitments made in 2024: to have a public-facing dashboard that reports on real-time crime center use and to develop “an omnibus surveillance technology policy.” SPD told researchers that both projects were delayed but in process, and Wilson announced at the press conference that both projects would be completed. Why SPD would need an outside agency like the NYU Policing Project to recommend they fulfill their own previous commitments remains unclear.

“It's disappointing how unscientific this whole process is,” Ryan Talen, a nurse at Harborview and member of Communities Not Cameras, told The Urbanist . “It doesn't even feel like there are standards. You know, we're just accepting the SPD's word after they say they're going to do something, they're not doing it, and we're still moving forward with the program. What does that tell us about who's calling the shots around here? Clearly, not the people that elected Katie Wilson.”

The auditors also recommended SPD institute a five-day data retention policy, given that’s what SPD say they already do in practice, and that they institute a data retention policy around the data they clip and attach to investigations so they don’t retain the data indefinitely, long after a particular investigation is closed.

“Video clips and other data stored on Evidence.com are retained by SPD indefinitely, resulting in a substantial and growing repository of data that outside agencies could seek to obtain,” the report reads. Evidence.com is Axon’s cloud-based evidence management system.

Another recommendation suggests that SPD should publish “in a clear and conspicuous location on its website” a full list of the tools and features it is using — and seeking approval to use — in its real-time crime center at least twice a year, as well as institute a policy for regular internal audits of the real-time crime center. In addition to internal audits, NYU researchers suggested the OIG should add identifying material changes to SPD’s use of surveillance tools to its annual audit requirements.

What the audit fails to address is what to do if SPD fails to implement these recommendations in practice. The OIG audit from October, for example, showed that SPD has already failed in its commitment to make sure every camera has privacy masking in place if it’s facing a private residence. And SPD has failed to live up to commitments it made in the Surveillance Impact Review back in 2024, even though two years have passed.

articles.title: Latest Look at 'Tactical Urbanism' Planned for Stadium District
articles.author: Ryan Packer
paras: A street transformation is coming to the Stadium District's front porch, with plans advancing for " tactical urbanism " along Occidental Avenue South near Lumen Field and T-Mobile Park. The quick-build changes tabbed for mid-2027 are intended to test a longer-term vision for a corridor that gets heavy usage on event days and is often trying to serve multiple different types of street users.
The Occidental Promenade is set to be the most visible product of Seattle's new People Streets and Public Spaces program, funded by the 2024 Seattle Transportation Levy .

Former Mayor Bruce Harrell directly inserted the promenade into his levy proposal, with support of stadium boosters including Seahawks chief operating officer David Young. The idea grew out of earlier efforts to improve Occidental Avenue, including a stadium district study that developed a streetscape plan in 2015, concepts that were ultimately put on a shelf to collect dust.

Final plans for the "near term" upgrades presented last week to Pioneer Square's Preservation District Board for approval show include chicanes, planters, street seating and micromobility corrals intended to carve out space along the wide street for pedestrian use. With the chicanes in place, the hope is for calmer traffic as drivers are prevented from picking up speed along a straight route of travel.

In a departure from most standard transportation projects, the Occidental Promenade is being managed by the Seattle Parks Foundation, in coordination with the Pioneer Square Alliance. The Seattle Department of Transportation (SDOT) will handle the design work. The Parks Foundation, a private non-profit organization that often bridges the gap between the City of Seattle and neighborhood groups interested in improving their park spaces, describes the promenade project as enabling a more "vibrant stadium district, providing street amenities and flexibility for the various users and venues."
The foundation also outlines a goal of better managing vending along the street. A future vending pilot program is expected to come back for separate approval at a later date.

"I would suggest it's probably the most hardworking street in downtown. We've got freight loading and unloading for the stadiums, which can range from, on a Taylor Swift concert, upwards of 20 to 25 semi trailers," said Jessa Timmer, Deputy Director at the Alliance for Pioneer Square, told the preservation board. "We've got pedestrian folks – during World Cup, we had, I don't even know how many, 150,000 to 200,000 pedestrians coming through Pioneer Square and this corridor. We've got back of house for many restaurants and businesses, sometimes front of house for those businesses."
"It's really a wide-ranging kind of ecosystem that's back here," Timmer said.

The improvements planned largely reinforce that ecosystem. The back-angle parking found across the street from Lumen Field will be retained, with a delineated walking path connecting the new nodes of pedestrian activity. Those paths will be most likely to be used on event days, creating a more orderly dispersal of pedestrian traffic when crowds are at their biggest.
It's less clear how utilized the planned seating will be on non-game days, with the street furniture essentially existing as an island in the middle of the street in some places.

"Our approach is really looking at a surface treatment and edge delineation to calm traffic and really work to improve that legibility and increase space for non-vehicular uses," SDOT project manager Ian Macek said.

The timeline to make the changes is currently dependent on Seattle City Light, which is planning work along Occidental in 2027, with promenade work to follow. But this phase will essentially act as a pilot to see how carving out pedestrian spaces works when it comes to the day-to-day operation of the street.

Though SDOT does need to receive a Certificate of Approval from the Pioneer Square Preservation Board to move forward with construction, that might not necessarily be the case with similar projects in the future. A legislative change put forward by Councilmember Alexis Mercedes Rinck would explicitly exempt traffic control devices from requirements for buy-in from historic district boards like Pioneer Square's. Though the change has received a fair amount of pushback from historic preservation advocates , it is still heading for a council vote by early next year.

"These these improvements are inspired by the neighborhood context," Macek said. "They are temporary and reversible, and so this is really seen as a way to help pilot some of these options to see how they work, and also help inform that longer term before we commit to a design and advance that forward to be able to test things out, and really looking at materials that aren't impacting the historic resources along the corridor."
While billed as a "quick-build" intervention, the Occidental Promenade will still take more than two years from the launch of planning in early 2025 to implementation in mid-2027.

Other People Streets and Public Spaces projects are also moving forward at SDOT, including pedestrian plazas planned in Upper Queen Anne, Admiral, and Delridge. Unlike Occidental, those projects weren't specifically named in the 2024 levy but grew out of neighborhood support for creating pedestrian-forward spaces, building on past programs like the Pavement to Parks program abandoned under former Mayor Jenny Durkan.

Final approval to move forward with the Occidental Promenade is expected at a Pioneer Square Preservation District Board meeting before the end of the year. You can review the full plan set for Occidental Avenue here . The department also has active surveys up on SW Lander Street , 18th Avenue SW , and W Crocket Street .

articles.title: Taskforce Spells Out Need for Cabinet-Level Housing Agency in Washington
articles.author: Ryan Packer
paras: A final report approved Tuesday by a 19-member taskforce implores the state legislature to take action to stand up a new housing department in 2027, identifying gaps and inefficiencies that are standing in the way of the state's housing goals. The proposed department would be led by a cabinet-level Secretary of Housing and charged with "owning" outcomes around market-rate and affordable housing, including the production of more than one million new homes expected to be needed over the next two decades.

The taskforce was the product of an executive order issued by Governor Bob Ferguson last year, charged with creating a "clear mission and vision" for a new statewide housing department after the idea had been floating around for years. Currently, most housing-focused work is housed (so to speak) within the state's Commerce Department, with that workload increasing significantly over recent years as the legislature created new land use mandates and accountability frameworks.

The taskforce was chaired by former state Senator David Frockt, who currently serves as Ferguson's Deputy Policy Director for Healthcare, Housing, and Public Safety. Other heavy-hitters on the panel included State Senator Jessica Bateman, Pierce County Executive Ryan Mello, and Lieutenant Governor Denny Heck.

"Our task was challenging: build the framework for a new governing system for housing, while doing nothing to distract from the ongoing housing work that must continue even as we stand up a new agency," Frockt wrote in an introductory letter embedded in the report. "[Our report] gives policymakers recommendations they can consider in 2027: one accountable agency, built in phases, without disrupting the programs that people depend on today."
Frockt framed a state housing czar as the missing ingredient in a recipe that was otherwise coming together.

"Washington has the people and the programs to build the homes we need," Frockt continued. "What we have lacked is one cabinet-level official leading a single results-oriented agency that interacts with other state actors and local public and private partners in a spirit of innovation, acceleration, and red tape removal."

Just last month, The Urbanist reported on new data showing that most housing growth targets around Central Puget Sound – an area that includes the state's largest growth centers – aren't being met, with overall rates of housing production since 2019 being carried by just a few jurisdictions, including Seattle. Of the 40 cities across King, Pierce, Snohomish and Kitsap Counties that are expected to accommodate the largest share of regional housing growth through 2044, just 14 are on track and many are significantly behind.

A spate of statewide housing reforms, including middle housing legalization, reduced parking requirements , and transit-oriented zoning mandates, have either gone into effect recently or set to be implemented in the coming years. Those reforms are expected to play a big role in moving the needle, but it will fall to the state to prod recalcitrant jurisdictions along.

One piece of that puzzle is the Housing Accountability Act , which reviews underperforming cities and towns on a rolling annual basis, provides guidance on how to get into compliance, and carries a major stick in the form of the "Builder's Remedy." Under that law, if a jurisdiction stays out-of-compliance with state law after being given an opportunity to make updates, they will have to approve any complete building permit as long as certain affordability thresholds are committed to, regardless of existing zoning.
So far, no Washington city has yet triggered it – although Bainbridge Island had flirted with testing the law.

"The recommendation responds to a housing system that produces too little housing despite substantial effort," the taskforce report's executive summary states. "To date, despite the more than 50 pieces of housing-related legislation that Washington has enacted in just the past five years, no state agency or the executive has established a single clear mission for a consolidated state housing department that encapsulates what the state is trying to do."

A phased implementation for the housing department would see a small startup team established alongside the housing secretary, using $5.38 million in seed funding in the next biennial budget. Four divisions would be established: data and performance, research and innovation, problem solving and partnerships, and standards and accountability. An initial strategic plan and an operating plan are both delivered during that phase, and a Washington Housing Results Council would be created and chaired by the secretary.

Phase two would occur during and after the 2028 legislative session, with programmatic functions and authorities officially moved into the new department and a "strategic housing action plan" established by that November. Phase three adds more programs and functions over time.

"With this phased approach, we're not waiting around for a new agency to build momentum and continue to advance the state's housing goals," said Amy Buckler, Assistant Director of Commerce's Housing Division. "We are concurrently working on the Washington Accelerator for Residential Production report, which is going to create a platform for building momentum and evolving. And we're doing that work concurrently with this."

Over the course of the taskforce's work, housing organizations of various stripes familiar with what it's like to navigate state government have weighed in on what could be achieved with a unified department, while clearly wanting to see more than a simple reorganization come out of the process.

"We believe the greatest benefit of this Department would be to serve as a visionary, central problem-solver and partner for affordable housing projects, the primary housing policy resource for the Legislature and Governor's Office, and a voice for the State in national housing policy discussions," Pamela Parr, President of the Washington Association of Housing Authorities, told the taskforce in letter this April. "In all these potential roles, the Department must be formed with an ingrained bias towards being a problem-solver in Washington State's housing framework, not a punitive enforcer of policy. This would be manifested in the vetting of projects (requiring skilled and knowledgeable staff), that once accepted, are supported by the Department in solving problems and removing barriers, even if those are from State policy."

With most of the big-ticket housing legislation checked off the legislature's to-do list, implementation and accountability will be a major focus over the coming years. The taskforce report clearly spells out a need for change, without proposing any bombshell changes that might make legislators skittish.

"I think that we have a practical, smart way forward that it can be recommended to Governor Ferguson to potentially propose to work with our colleagues in the legislature, both from a budgetary and policy standpoint," Frockt said ahead of a final vote to adopt the report. "We'll see how it all plays out in the current budget environment, but it's a smart, appropriate way forward that doesn't, I think, bite off too much initially, but also sets the stage for good work to come."

articles.title: Rinck seeks five council votes to block Capitol Hill and Central District camera rollout until SPD addresses risks
articles.author: Justin Carder
paras: City Councilmember Alexis Mercedes Rinck is calling for support for her budget proviso that would pause the expansion of Seattle’s Real Time Crime Center police cameras until recommendations from the Office of the Inspector General are satisfied.

The move follows Mayor Katie Wilson’s decision to lift her pause on the expansion as Seattle Police officials say they are working to respond to a privacy audit of the system identified constitutional risks, technological shortfalls, and policy gaps. Recent reviews under the Office of Inspector General made similar findings .

Saying she has “deep concerns about surveillance technology from civil rights implications, policy oversight gaps, and the efficacy of this technology,” Rinck said Wednesday that the proviso is supported by South Seattle Councilmember Eddie Lin and Rinck’s fellow citywide representative Dionne Foster but requires five votes to pass.
“Final votes in budget start on Friday. Now is the time to make your voice heard,” Rinck posted in her social media statement on the proposal.

The Office of Inspector General recommended that the Seattle Police Department implement case numbers and formal justifications within the Axon Fusus software before analysts can view camera feeds to prevent unauthorized or proactive surveillance. It also urged the department and city leaders to establish clear policies and privacy safeguards for integrating privately owned security cameras, including geographic boundaries, protocols to avoid monitoring non-public spaces, and retention limits, while enforcing stricter search logging and civil liberty controls across stored surveillance databases like Automated License Plate Readers.

The Seattle City Council is wrapping up the city’s long budget season with final adjustments to the mayor’s 2027-2028 budget plan including tapping $31 million in JumpStart payroll tax reserves and cutting $22 million in pension transfers to reverse cuts proposed by the mayor to address a looming budget deficit.

CHS reported in March as Wilson followed up on campaign promises and stopped an expansion of the city’s police camera system to the stadium district, Capitol Hill’s nightlife areas, and 23rd Ave in the Central District citing concerns about how law enforcement and federal authorities might access the technology and data.
The cameras for Capitol Hill — budgeted but never installed — would cover Broadway from Capitol Hill Station to Pike/Pine and the core of the Pike/Pine nightlife zone.

In the Central District, the camera system will be centered around safety at Garfield High School with boundaries running from a block north of the school along E Cherry all the way to S Jackson. The western edge has been planned to include 20th Ave and the eastern edge would extend along 26th Ave.

The Capitol Hill system is estimated to cost around $400,000 to install and $35,000 a year to operate. The Central District installation has a budget of $425,000 and also an estimated $35,000 in “ongoing annual costs.”

articles.title: 1,000+ reports a year — Sweeps in Cal Anderson Park are rare but neighborhood encampment complaints tell a different story
articles.author: Justin Carder
paras: Tents along the east edge of the park included in an October clearance report — one of three clearances logged in 2026

Facing escalating neighborhood friction around Capitol Hill’s central park, the Greater Seattle Business Association has pushed back against City Hall , calling for a halt to homeless encampment removals in Cal Anderson .

The pushback comes as Mayor Katie Wilson says she is shifting the city’s encampment strategy to prioritize clearance of public spaces like sidewalks and parks while pairing the efforts with increased services and shelter.

In a statement addressed to the mayor, the LGBTQ+ and allied business advocacy group that bills itself as Capitol HIll’s chamber of commerce challenged the assertion that restaurant, shop, and property owners have asked for stepped-up enforcement.

“We request that Mayor Wilson immediately order a pause on all sweeps of Cal Anderson Park until this issue is meaningfully resolved,” the letter states, signed by GSBA Capitol Hill Neighborhood Safety Manager Jen Carl and Policy and Advocacy Director Gabriel Neuman .
The leadership pushed back directly against city outreach teams:

It has also come to our attention that the Unified Care Team has been referencing the business community to justify harmful encampment removals that do not adhere to the policies and laws set forth by the city. This statement is both inappropriate and inaccurate. While some individuals may support these initiatives, our overall Capitol Hill community, including the vast majority of our business owners, firmly oppose such punitive and unnecessary measures.

The GSBA expressed alarm over “harassment and intimidation of our unhoused trans and LGBTQ+ siblings” by the Unified Care Team and Seattle Police Department officers, urging an independent review alongside expanded harm-reduction investments like handwashing stations, sharps containers, and funding for mutual aid and community groups including Stone Soup Crew, MANTIS, and the Cal Anderson Park Alliance.
Earlier this year , CHS reported on CAPA calling on the city to increase maintenance and outreach resources at the park citing public safety concerns.
GSBA’s new demand for an immediate pause in sweeps comes as city records shows relatively rare full clearance activity in the park.
According to “Site Journal” records published by the Seattle Human Services Department , the city has logged only three formal encampment clearances for Cal Anderson in all of 2026:

By comparison, the city logged two site journals for the park in 2025 (August and December) and only one in 2023, with none archived under Cal Anderson in the portal between 2017 and 2022 or throughout 2024.

While daily field contacts, bag-and-tag garbage runs, and park ranger moves can occur without triggering a formal HSD site journal, full-scale removal operations in Cal Anderson have officially averaged just one every few months.
Though clearance logs show infrequent full sweeps, citizen reports from the ground tell a different story.
Data from the city’s Find It Fix It customer service portal tracking reported unauthorized encampments reveals an aggressive rebound in complaints surrounding the park in 2026:
The records show where community tension concentrates. Rather than spreading across the park’s interior lawns, reports are pinned to perimeter sidewalks and transit borders:
Meanwhile, Seattle City Hall is setting the spending plan for 2027 including how the city will step up its own efforts as the King County Regional Homelessness Authority is ramped down .

A key debate focuses on the the Unified Care Team and Wilson’s plan which preserves core funding for rapid encampment and obstruction removals versus City Council efforts to impose stricter oversight and push resources toward harm reduction. Facing a significant deficit balanced in part by tapping JumpStart payroll expense tax reserves, council members and community stakeholders are pushing budget provisos that would condition the team’s funding on reporting regarding shelter referral outcomes, property storage compliance, and law enforcement costs.
Council proposals could open spending on new handwashing stations and public toilets and closer operational alignment with the CARE department’s unarmed alternative crisis response teams.

The Wilson administration is slowing its homelessness and shelter goals as part of spending shifts to address a projected $175 million budget deficit. While Wilson’s core goals remain in place including the establishment of approximately 1,000 emergency shelter spaces paired with wraparound services, budget realities will mean a slower approach.
Wilson also vetoed a plan to create a RV parking permit system tied to shelter and services, saying it would not be a cost-effective program.

Earlier this year, the administration framed the delivery of 1,000 shelter units as a single-year objective for 2026. The administration has now extended that goal through the end of 2027, scheduling 960 total beds to serve an estimated 1,750 people annually across facilities established in 2026 and eight sites slated for 2027.

According to a 2026 count across King County , the number of unsheltered individuals jumped from around 9,800 in 2024 to 11,829 in 2026, a 21% increase in people living on the streets, in vehicles, or in parks.
In the meantime, neighbors and passersby are logging nearly three encampment reports a day this year in Cal Anderson Park.

articles.title: Suspect arrested after attempted luring incident at Garfield High School
articles.author: CHS Staff
paras: A man was arrested Tuesday morning after allegedly attempting to lure a Garfield High School student in the campus parking lot, school administrators announced.

The incident occurred around 10:40 AM Tuesday when a vehicle pulled into the 23rd Ave school’s parking lot as a student was walking onto campus. The male driver reportedly attempted to entice the student. The student was not harmed and immediately reported the encounter to school authorities.

articles.title: Dick’s still sells burgers but its new Broadway neighbor Rizzo’s will bring yet more chicken to Capitol Hill
articles.author: Justin Carder
paras: TikTok guy Nick Rizzo breaking the Broadway chicken news

News is where you find it these days so it should not be hugely surprising that details of yet another new combatant in the coming war for chicken supremacy across Capitol Hill and the Central District comes from a Seattle reality star’s TikTok video we saw on Youtube thanks to a CHS reader.

Rizzo’s Crispy Chicken is lined up to be yet another new Capitol Hill-area chicken joint with a new restaurant taking shape on Broadway. The space was most recently home to the Don’t Yell At Me bubble tea shop that shuttered earlier this year in — we’re not making this up — a suite left empty by the exit of one of the two Broadway ZoomCare locations. Paperwork filed over the summer after the tea joint’s closure provided a few clues about what was coming next as the suite was prepared with the addition of a new “3 phase 50A circuit” for a deep fryer.
Next to Dick’s Drive-in , Rizzo’s could be set up for success next to the Hill’s busiest food joint. A McDonald’s at Broadway and E Olive Way would only add to the area’s fast food draw.

According to permit filings, Rizzo’s is being opened by Seattle area entrepreneur Samer Shammar who is also apparently opening another location in the Pinehurst commercial strip where he grew a smoke shop business.

Rizzo’s is part of what will surely lead to the great Central Seattle chicken war of 2027 as newcomers like Port of Peri Peri Chicken and the San Francisco-born Starbird Chicken chain on E Pike in a portion of the block’s emptied Amazon grocery store join a comically robust flock of chicken-related eateries opening across the area.

Industry reports say chicken concepts deliver resilient profit margins and simplified kitchen prep, keeping down food and labor costs against rising overhead in cities like Seattle and growing neighborhoods like the Central District and Capitol Hill.
It also helps that chicken holds up well for delivery.
As for TikTok Seattle dude Nick Rizzo , the in the works chicken joint

Unlike influencer Matt Broussard who has signed on to help Seattle restaurant group Conscious Hospitality Group launch Char the Chicken , a “fire-grilled rotisserie chicken” concept, in the group’s former chicken sandwich chain’s spot opening on 11th Ave, TikTok Seattle dude Nick Rizzo’s relationship to Rizzo’s seems like only some fun content for the influencer without any crunchy chicken skin in the game.
Rizzo’s Crispy Chicken will open soon at 125 Broadway E.

articles.title: Pop Loser: Macklemore Says Climate Pledge Arena Won’t Host His Free Palestine Tour
articles.author: Audrey Vann
paras: Welcome back to Pop Loser! This week, Macklemore says that nine US arenas turned down his Free Palestine tour, U2’s The Edge (reportedly) wrote a sequel to Elf, and Television guitarist Richard Lloyd passed away. Plus, I’ll discuss why I actually prefer Adventure over Marquee Moon.
This week in Strangerland, Dave Segal attended the first annual Baba Obscura festival and covered every band he saw, including Mdou Moctar, the Gories, Zookraught, the Black Tones, and more.

Macklemore says Climate Pledge Arena rejected hosting his Free Palestine tour. On Friday, the rapper shared that booking shows in the US for his benefit tour has been increasingly difficult, with nine major venues turning him down, including the Amazon-owned Seattle arena. “We received available dates at these arenas through the end of the year. But once they found out these were my benefit shows for Palestine, those dates were suddenly off the table,” he wrote. “The doors were closed. The conversations were all different, but the result was the same. These shows were not going to be allowed to happen in these venues. In over twenty years of touring, I’ve never experienced anything like this.”

RIP Richard Lloyd . Co-founding guitarist of the pioneering New York punk band Television died on Saturday at the age of 75, after a battle with cholangiocarcinoma, a rare bile duct cancer. Tributes celebrating the late guitarist included one by the Smiths’s Johnny Marr, who wrote : “A seeker and finder and a true inspiration with and without the guitar. It was an honour to know him and a blessing to have been a fan.”

New guy just dropped: On Thursday, the French Canadian polka-dotted experimental rock duo Angine de Pointrine debuted a third member at their show in Toronto. The new unnamed triangle-player sports a large rectangular head with gold horns and a long protruding nose. It is unclear if this is a one-time thing or not—the band’s publicist told Pitchfork that they were not sure.

Apparently, the Edge wrote a sequel to Elf . And no, this isn’t a fake headline I created using Mad Libs. Comedian and actor Andy Richter (who plays a small role in Elf ) revealed to Obsessed: The Podcast that the film’s producer was contacted by the U2 guitarist about a script he’d written for Elf 2 . “It’s the weirdest story, but apparently it was fully written,” said Richter. “Somewhere in the world there is an Edge-penned Elf 2 out there. I would love for that to make the light of day.” The Edge has yet to comment. U2 is appearing in this column more than I am comfortable with lately, but this needed to be addressed.

Before I knew what inspired this new single by Portland-based singer-songwriter Katherine Paul (aka Black Belt Eagle Scout), I could feel its sense of freedom through its pulsing rhythm and carefree lyrics: “Fuck you / Fuck your ideals / Fuck what you have to say / I’m done with you / I just want to be free / And listen to the trees.” Paul began writing the song while transitioning out of a 9-to-5 job in the Native nonprofit world and into making music full time. “I was feeling burnt out and wanted a life where I could spend more time making music and being free outside in the trees,” she shared on Instagram .

I always hear people raving about Television’s 1977 debut Marquee Moon (and for good reason—it’s an undeniable classic), but never about their 1978 follow-up, Adventure. Like the respective album covers—the band in stark high-contrast, eyes leveled at the camera on Marquee versus the relaxed, almost soft demeanor of Adventure —the sound on their sophomore album is lighter, breezier, and relieves the tension built up on their debut. Front to back, the album is flawless and includes some of their prettiest, softest moments on “Days,” “Carried Away,” and “The Dream’s Dream.”

articles.title: Nobody Wants a McDonald’s in Chinatown
articles.author: Guy Oron
paras: McDonald’s wants to put a new store in Seattle’s Chinatown-International District (CID). Almost nobody thinks that’s a good idea. They are decidedly not loving it.

Last night, about 80 CID residents and supporters packed the meeting of the International Special Review District (ISRD), the neighborhood’s historic preservation board. Impassioned public comments, handmade protest signs in Chinese and English, and several people in Ronald McDonald-esque clown masks injected the typically sleepy meeting with life.

McDonald’s wants to place its new franchise on the corner of 4th Avenue South and South Jackson Street, along a busy thoroughfare close to the regional transit hub and sports stadiums. The storefront has remained vacant since Bartell Drugs closed four years ago.

In submitting its proposal , Mickey D’s managed a remarkable feat: Uniting the community to take action in the span of less than a week. At the ISRD meeting, the only people who spoke in favor of the new store were McDonald’s employees and the landlord’s property manager.

Concerns from neighbors ranged from the impact McDonald’s would have on other restaurants in the CID to the company’s incongruity with the Asian character of the neighborhood to worries it could attract homeless people and drug users.

“We want something that represents and takes care of this neighborhood,” said Karen Sakata Akada, owner of iconic karaoke bar Bush Garden. “All the small businesses, not large corporations, is part of what makes this neighborhood special.”

State Rep.-elect Kelabe Tewolde and Seattle City Councilmember Alexis Mercedes Rinck also attended the meeting to show their opposition. The ISRD board received more than 100 written comments in opposition to the proposed McDonald’s.
A consultant for the company gave a presentation on the proposed store’s design and exterior, saying it would bring 60 new jobs and activate the vacant commercial space.

It’s not the first time McDonald’s has tried to bring Happy Meals to the CID. In 2000, the corporation tried to open a store on 5th Avenue S and Jackson Street, only to withdraw after vociferous community opposition.

City and state law requires McDonald’s to obtain the ISRD’s approval to proceed with its development in the historic district. Board member Huy Pham indicated that the fast food giant would be unlikely to get it.

“I think you did your job in presenting and providing the pro forma behind why McDonald’s and the property owner might choose this proposal,” Pham told the consultant. “But there isn’t really anything you can modify to gain mine or a community consensus to approve. So I would suggest saving your time and money on moving with a different project.”

articles.title: Slog AM: Car Goes up Light Rail Tracks Again, Katie Wilson’s Bad Surveillance Decision, Sen. Chuck Schumer Needs to Throw In the Towel
articles.author: Charles Mudede
paras: Let’s begin AM with my November 9 Odyssey . After teaching a night class at Cornish College of the Arts, a film class that concerned the Soviet Montage school (we discussed Man With a Movie Camera by Dziga Vertov), I walked down to the corner of Westlake Avenue and Denny Avenue and waited for the locally famous ( and infamous ) 8 bus to transport me up to Capitol Hill. The time: 6:10 p.m. But the bus, which now has a dedicated lane, was a whopping 13 minutes behind time. And the bus behind it was also growing late. Because the same thing happened to me the week before, and the week before that, I had to repress my doubts about Mayor Katie Wilson’s new lane.

Now, here’s the funny part , cars heading up Denny Avenue enjoyed a freedom of movement that never existed at this hour when the extra lane was all theirs and not devoted to the 8 bus. But all of this can only amount to a hill of beans because it’s a personal impression of the current situation. I will attempt in the near future to determine if my experience has any value in traffic data collected by the Seattle Department of Transportation or King County Metro.

Part two of Monday’s Odyssey. articles.title: Seattle Mayor Expands Police Camera Surveillance Today, With No Privacy Safeguards in 2026
articles.author: Cedar Attanasio
paras: Mayor Katie Wilson gave an emphatic “yes” to the immediate expansion of police surveillance in Seattle on Tuesday, with no immediate policies to reduce the risk of abuse by local and federal law enforcement power in 4 to 6 months.

The decision follows nearly a year of foot-dragging over expanding, freezing, or gutting the city’s police camera network and the release of a related report she commissioned from New York University. It’s the clearest departure from Wilson’s campaign promise to “Trump-proof Seattle.”

The city’s police surveillance network includes around 600 cameras integrated into an erroneously named “Real Time Crime Center.” The cameras from the Seattle Police Department could help in a crisis, in real time, but the civil liberties concerns raised mostly stem from their other main use: recording video footage for police analysts to comb through later.
And starting this week, the footage will grow and grow.

“The Stadium District cameras were installed prior to the World Cup and will be turned on immediately,” Wilson told reporters Tuesday, adding that “The others still need to be purchased and installed, and we don’t know exactly how long that’s going to take because we’re at the whims of the, you know, postal service or whatever.”
Future expansions of the digital dragnet will include areas around Garfield High School and Capitol Hill.

That footage is vulnerable to hacking, misuse by police workers for stalking, secret federal subpoenas to contractors, overt federal subpoenas to the city, and public records requests from anyone, from pro-life activists to ICE agents.
If Wilson was trying to strike a balance between police investigative power and individual liberty, she fell on her face.

Wilson enumerated her commitment to a dozen of the report’s recommendations (more SPD accountability, rules for surveilling protests, limits to online data retention), but not on the same timeline. Big Sister’s expansion will happen immediately, while transparency is TBD.

“At the same time, and crucially, my office and SPD will be working urgently to implement most of the recommendations in this audit,” she said, adding a much murkier timeline of “over the next four to six months.”

At least one of the recommendations she committed to, a public dashboard on the surveillance web’s usage, was recommended to complete no later than three months after the report’s release. Other recommendations she dodged, like requiring a warrant for tracking individuals across cameras except under narrow and urgent circumstances.

Under the mayor’s plan, the city’s surveillance will expand, while possible access by hostile actors like Immigration and Customs Enforcement officials will remain the same: mainly through public records requests (including under pseudonyms) and subpoenas, which can be done without the city’s knowledge.

“There is not a lot in SPD’s control over preventing that information, including information that might be used for civil immigration enforcement or for protected healthcare, from leaving its custody through those two channels,” says Clare Garvie one of the authors of the report NYU School of Law’s Policing Project.
The report did not quantify the risks, and left it to public leaders to decide on whether to take them.
To date, there are no reported instances of federal agents using Seattle’s video records. But the report recommended that city policies get ahead of changing technology and legal landscape.
“My assessment, based on the audit, is that the risk is very low. I mean, I think in general, ICE has its own ways of getting information and does not need our camera footage,” Wilson told reporters.
It’s great news for folks who supported Wilson’s centrist, millionaire opponent, Bruce Harrell.

“To ensure safe communities across all Seattle neighborhoods, businesses, and diverse stakeholders, we must effectively leverage this technology like other major cities across the country,” District 7 Councilmember Bob Kettle, chair of the Public Safety Committee, said in a statement Tuesday.
But Wilson’s assessment, and the resulting decision, did not land with former supporters.

“She did this the same week that Stephen Miller became Chief of Staff to Trump,” says Xochitl Maykovich anti-cameras activist and former Wilson campaign field co-director . “The master of the deportation machine.”
Wilson put out a video Tuesday timed with her announcement that underscored that the surveillance web she’s expanding doesn’t include Flock cameras, which read licence plates ( for ICE ).
“These are not Flock cameras,” Wilson said. “This is a different system, managed by a different company.”

The different company is Axon , the company that sends much of SPD’s video to remote data centers has over $100 million in federal contracts on Miller’s puppet strings, including $37 million with ICE, according to USAspending.gov

Miller is the master because he’s helped Trump pull the levers of power to do illegal stuff, over and over again, far beyond something as simple as asking Axon to hand over some municipal data. This is not a man who respects the Constitution, let alone Axon’s terms of services with our city.

Maykovich says she forwarded an ACLU post about Seattle surveillance privacy issues to Wilson during her 2025 campaign, and it wound up as part of her platform : “I vow to protect our neighbors and defend Seattle’s status as a sanctuary city ” and “Seattle can’t be a true sanctuary city if ICE can access data about you through City policies and programs that could have been better designed.
Wilson declined to comment on how her decision related to those promises.
“This is a betrayal of her base,” Maykovich says.

articles.title: The forgotten history of the New York City Marathon
articles.author: Alison Mariella Désir
paras: Last week, I successfully ran the New York City Marathon! It was perfect weather and I surprised myself by feeling great the entire race. Along the course I saw so many of my friends out there cheering; I smiled, I laughed, I cried. My favorite moment was coming up to the Harlem Run cheer station and seeing my son there holding a BIG photo of my head!
I founded Harlem Run 13 years ago, and seeing the running movement continue to thrive fills me with such joy. This year, 62 members of Harlem Run completed the marathon!

Going back to New York, going back home, is always reenergizing but this year was particularly special because it was the 50 th anniversary of the five-borough marathon course. Prior to 1976, the New York City marathon was run entirely on loops inside Central Park. What many people don’t know is that it was Ted Corbitt, a Black man, who had the idea to move the marathon outside of Central Park.

Ted Corbitt, also known as the father of long-distance running, was one of the most accomplished long-distance runners of all time. He completed 223 marathons and ultramarathons in his lifetime and was the first African American Olympic marathoner (Helsinki, 1952) and the founding president of New York Road Runners (1958–1960). In 1976, he proposed that the New York City Marathon be hosted outside of the park and through the five boroughs.

Percy Sutton, Manhattan Borough President and former Freedom Rider, served on the New York City Marathon’s Honorary Board of Advisors and as chairman of the Marathon Committee, a group of NYRR officials and other runners. Sutton heard Corbitt’s idea and proposed the race begin on Staten Island and cross over the Verrazzano-Narrows Bridge – something many people that was impossible. But Sutton was the type of person who made the impossible possible. He went on to secure the initial $25,000 in funding to help bring the race to life.

For almost 50 years, the origin story of the New York City Marathon has been obscured. Other people have claimed the race was their idea; most people left out Percy Sutton’s name. And so, it has been important for me, as a runner and lover of history, to help set the record straight. I began doing so through the telling of this history in my book, Running While Black , and this year, I was able to host a panel before the marathon featuring Crystal Howard, Chief Communications and Community Office of NYRR, Gary Corbitt, historian and son of Ted Corbitt, and Keisha James-Sutton, granddaughter of Percy Sutton. In the words of Gary Corbitt, history is fragile, and it often gets lost. Now that you’ve heard this story – it's your duty to help set the record straight.

Stay tuned – I'll be announcing two exciting Out and Back events very soon: an Out and Back screening in February and the Explore! Family Fair in March.
