articles.title: What Medicaid and ACA cuts mean for Washington
articles.author: Venice Buhain
paras: After last year's passage of HR1, the One Big Beautiful Bill put in place several changes that will decrease enrollment in Apple Health, Washington’s Medicaid program. Congress made changes to Medicaid to offset tax cuts in the 2025 bill.

One change is that adults aged 19 to 64 will have to work, train, or perform community service for at least 80 hours per month to keep their Apple Health coverage. Exceptions include being pregnant, being a primary caregiver, or having a medical condition. That requirement starts on Jan. 1. Furthermore, people in the program will have to prove their eligibility every six months, instead of every year.
Another change is that noncitizen adults like refugees and asylees who had been eligible for coverage will no longer be covered by Medicaid.
That means about 200,000 people in Washington state will lose their free or low-cost health coverage.

Ryan Moran, director of the Washington Health Care Authority, said that the state has taken measures to help people navigate the increased requirements, which will help about 400,000 of the 600,000 adults who would be affected stay on the program.
“But let us make no mistake, there will absolutely be coverage losses,” Moran said.

“The full effect of this will not be known until the end of 2027, and we at the state are trying to do everything that we can to preserve and mitigate coverage loss as these changes take effect,” he said.

And that’s not all. The changes also require states to reduce their supplemental funding to medical providers that are contracted to provide care to Medicaid patients. That is estimated to be a loss of $1.5 billion to Washington hospitals starting in 2028 -- which could mean higher costs for other patients either due to private insurance costs going up or hospitals having to rely more on charity care.
“That's more expensive for everyone, right?” Moran said.
Open enrollment for 2027 on the Washington Health Benefit Exchange is open and in the past few years, federal changes have made big impacts to health coverage accessibility in Washington state.

The first is the cuts to Medicaid, which provides health coverage for about 1.5 million adults and children in Washington state. Those cuts were included in what Trump called the One Big Beautiful Bill, which passed in 2025. Another is the continued impact of the loss of tax credits for people who purchase insurance through the Washington Health Benefit Exchange.
Recently, Sen. Patty Murray held a press conference to address these changes and how it will affect people as they sign up for health insurance in open enrollment.

“We've been knowing this coming. I've been talking to doctors and providers and health care clinics and hospitals all over our state about what that was going to mean to them. And now we are going to see the impact on people's health insurance when they pay for them,” Murray said.
The press conference was held a few days before the election.

At the press conference, Washington Insurance Commissioner Patty Kuderer added that on top of the loss of tax credits for marketplace health insurance, premiums are also rising, with an average increase of 22%.

“Nearly 280,000 people buy health coverage here if they don't get insurance through their employer, and most do so through our own state-based exchange,” Kuderer said. “And today, many people are feeling the sticker shock of the increased premiums.”
Murray said addressing health care costs would be one priority for Democrats in Congress.
“When we get back, we have to make sure that we work to reinstate the tax credits and fight to take these Medicaid cuts back,” she said.

Since H.R. 1 – the so-called “One Big Beautiful Bill Act,” - passed last summer, cuts to Medicare and Medicaid have impacted hospitals and patients across the country. Rural hospitals in Washington are bracing for the latest round of cuts that kick in January 1 st .

Three Rivers Hospital in Brewster covers the largest land area of any hospital district in Washington - about 2,500 square miles in the state’s Okanogan region. More than two-thirds of their patients are Medicaid or Medicare.

Starting in October, some immigrants, refugees and asylum seekers were no longer eligible for Medicaid. Starting on January 1 st , many Medicaid recipients will need to show that they are working, volunteering or in school at least 80 hours a a month. Plus, they will need to reapply every six months.

“Once the changes hit next year, although we’re not quite sure how it’s going to affect us, we know there are folks that are no longer eligible for Medicaid, and we need to be able to respond to that and help them to maintain the coverage,” said Three Rivers Hospital Chief Operating Officer Jamie Boyer.

Three Rivers says they’ve already had to take on more bad debt and charity care since H.R. 1 passed in 2025, and rural health transformation funding hasn’t made up for the losses. They’ve also seen some Medicare Advantage plans offered by private insurances leave the region. The hospital says they’re more worried than ever that the newest cuts could force a worst-case scenario – cutting services, or even closing the hospital.

“We don’t have a magic crystal ball, so we don’t know of all the struggles we will have moving forward. But we just know that we have a strong team here, and we know that we can get through tough times,” Boyer said.

articles.title: A Newborn Died in a Faith-Healing Sect. The State — and One Ex-Believer — Stepped in to Save Her Twin.
articles.author: Noelle Crombie
paras: The deputy medical examiner thought the family was being evasive. Eric Tonsfeldt had been dispatched to the pistachio-green house in Oregon City on the night of March 5, 2017. Inside he found Sarah Mitchell in bed, her dead newborn in her arms.

Mitchell is a member of the Followers of Christ, a sect known for refusing medical treatment. She had received no prenatal care. Three women without medical training guided her delivery that afternoon.

Tonsfeldt listened as the family insisted that the baby, whom they had named Ginnifer, had seemed healthy for most of the afternoon, then suddenly stopped breathing. They couldn’t explain why the baby appeared so underweight. Their answers to many of Tonsfeldt’s questions were vague. Nobody would make eye contact with him.

Later, investigators would discover that 13 minutes after Ginnifer’s birth, Followers began exchanging a series of worried texts. “Not good breathing,” one wrote in a group chat. Another requested prayers: “She’s really bad.” (One person in the chat would later advise deleting the messages.)

No one had called 911 as the gaps between each breath increased. When asked why not, Ginnifer’s father later said, “Because it’s in God’s hands.” He anointed his daughter with olive oil and wept as he prayed that she would be OK. Ginnifer died in his arms at 7 p.m., four hours after she was born.
Tonsfeldt gently collected the newborn and examined her in another room. She weighed 3½ pounds, roughly half that of an average full-term infant. He found no signs of injury or trauma.

The medical examiner still felt that something was awry. To play for time, he asked if someone would make him a cup of coffee and headed to the kitchen. As Tonsfeldt waited, one of the baby’s grandfathers approached him and blurted out an unexpected question: Would it make a difference if Ginnifer had a twin?
There was another baby, a girl named Evelyn. She was alive.
In the dim light of a bathroom, Tonsfeldt found women huddled over a tiny newborn, who was barely making a sound. They were feeding her from an eyedropper.

He told the family to get her to a hospital. After Evelyn’s grandfather made it clear they weren’t going anywhere, Tonsfeldt summoned the police, who delivered an ultimatum: Take Evelyn to the hospital or they’d do it themselves.

Evelyn’s family relented. A patrol car followed to make sure they got there. She was admitted to a neonatal intensive care unit in Portland with respiratory distress syndrome. With the help of a breathing machine and a feeding tube, Evelyn began to stabilize. An autopsy would later conclude the same condition, common in premature babies, had caused her sister’s death.
The Mitchells were charged with murder by neglect, as well as criminal mistreatment for failing to get Evelyn medical care. That left authorities with another challenge: Who would care for Evelyn?

Her family assumed any custody arrangement would be temporary and suggested Marshall and Jennifer Phillips, a couple born and raised in the Followers. But Marshall was no ordinary Follower. Once, when his young son became gravely ill, he brought him to a hospital. In the eyes of the state, that made Marshall and his wife suitable candidates to look after Evelyn.

Evelyn’s family didn’t know then that Marshall’s choice to save his son had set him on a yearslong journey, one that would eventually lead him away from the only life he’d ever known. And that he would take Evelyn with him.

For more than a century, states have wrestled with how to address the deaths of children whose parents refuse them medical care for religious reasons. As early as 1901, a father in New York who believed in the “power of God to heal the sick through prayer” was prosecuted for failing to call a doctor for his young daughter who died from pneumonia. Since then, courts have repeatedly held — in cases where Christian Scientists refused treatment or Jehovah’s Witnesses declined blood transfusions — that adults are free to reject medical care for themselves.
Whether they can be compelled to provide medical care for their children is another matter, one that’s been left to states to decide. Courts have generally deferred to legislatures on this question.

Marshall Phillips was raised in the Followers of Christ, which forbids medical care. When his son fell gravely ill, he took him to the hospital. That choice set him on a yearslong journey, one that would eventually lead him away from the only life he’d ever known.

For decades, Oregon’s law gave latitude to faith healing and authorities did little to intervene. Between 1989 and 1999, 18 children of the Oregon City-based Followers died. (The sect numbered between 1,500 and 2,000 at its peak.) Most or all of those deaths were preventable, according to the state medical examiner at the time, who estimated that the child death rate in the sect was 26 times that of the general population.

The revelation of those deaths, in The Oregonian and other news outlets, prompted state lawmakers to act. In 1999, they removed spiritual treatment as a defense for second-degree manslaughter and criminal mistreatment. In 2008, prosecutors filed their first case against Followers parents after a 15-month-old died from untreated bronchial pneumonia and a blood infection. A jury convicted the girl’s father of a single count of criminal mistreatment, a misdemeanor, and acquitted her mother.

Two more children in the sect died without medical attention during this period, prompting the Legislature in 2011 to do away with the spiritual defense for any crime. Among those supporting the change: the Christian Science church, which by then had softened its stance amid a steep decline in membership. In a letter to lawmakers that year, a church official wrote: “Spiritual care should never be practiced at the expense of a child’s life.”

Changes in Oregon law — and prosecutors’ willingness to pursue parents who watched their children die — spurred a slow but perceptible shift: Deaths of children in the Followers have become an anomaly. Ginnifer Mitchell’s death in 2017 came amid that yearslong decline. Since then, one child has died due to lack of medical care.

During this same time frame in Idaho, where the laws protect parents who rely only on faith healing, reporting by ProPublica found at least 11 babies and children of Followers died from treatable conditions.

Still, Ginnifer’s death shows how the most entrenched elements of faith-healing communities resist aggressive enforcement. Sarah Mitchell chose to give birth without doctors or nurses, even as her sister was in prison for failing to provide medical care for her premature newborn, who died in 2009. And Sarah’s lack of prenatal care was such that she realized she was carrying twins only when her labor continued after her first baby emerged.
Evelyn might not have survived if police didn’t have the law on their side, allowing them to intervene and demand that her parents take her to the hospital.

The stories of Evelyn and Marshall Phillips — still the subject of legal proceedings today — offer a rare view into the closed community and reveal both the power and the limits of the state’s efforts to compel parents to seek medical care for their children.

Marshall’s ancestors were among the earliest members of the Followers, whose history dates to the late 1800s, when faith-healing sects were active in the Midwest. The faithful later migrated west, starting congregations in Idaho. In the 1930s, a charismatic Followers preacher named Walter White left Idaho for Oregon City, then a lively hub for the timber and paper industries. White’s emotional sermons earned him the moniker “the crying preacher.”

Followers believed the devout earned their place in the afterlife through good acts. They also believed that God heals. The doctrine stems from a passage in the Book of James, which proclaims “And the prayer of faith shall save the sick, and the Lord shall raise him up.” Seeking medical care was viewed as an abandonment of faith. Those who visited doctors risked being shunned.
By the 1950s, White broke ties with other Followers congregations. He later said that Christ had visited him in a dream and told him the world would soon end and so would baptisms.

White died in 1969 at age 67. Baptisms ended after that, effectively sealing the faithful from the outside world. The Followers never identified White’s successor. To this day, the congregation has no pastor. The lack of a spiritual leader seems only to have intensified members’ influence on one another.
The sect’s practices include other unusual elements: The Bible doesn’t figure in their services, which consist mostly of congregants singing hymns.

In many respects, Followers lead conventional lives. As a boy born in 1975, Marshall rode his bike, ate sugary treats, watched TV and listened to 1980s rock bands like Van Halen. His parents took him and his siblings camping and saved up for trips to Disneyland.

But his life was also circumscribed by his faith. Several times a week, he accompanied his parents to functions at the beige meetinghouse set back from busy Molalla Avenue in Oregon City. Starting at age 7, Followers’ children are separated by gender and age into their own pews. Marshall understood that he would grow up, and grow old, with the kids seated around him. He was instructed not to befriend kids outside the church. Followers considered them “worldly,” the sect’s derisive term for those focused on terrestrial, rather than celestial, concerns.

Like his peers, Marshall never visited a pediatrician. He was never vaccinated. His mom anointed his forehead with extra virgin olive oil when his head throbbed. He endured chicken pox and whooping cough and eventually recovered from both — proof, he believed, of God’s healing powers.
His parents, like others in the sect, made exceptions for dental care. They accepted the use of Novocain but refused the ibuprofen the dentist recommended to address lingering pain after a procedure.

Marshall knew from a young age that his future would be determined by the church. He figured he’d work for a Follower. He’d marry one, too. Marshall and Jennifer went on their first date in a courtship ritual the Followers call a carload — small groups of teens who drive together to get ice cream or coffee. She was 14 and he was 18. They married when Jennifer turned 17, the age girls in the Followers typically wed.

Jennifer’s father had died the year before, surrounded by men from the church. Members were expected to care for the dying, with men tending to men and women to women. Her father never went to the doctor, and family members think he died from heart failure. He was 37.

Women typically give birth in their parents’ homes, and Jennifer was no exception. She delivered her first child, Mary, in the living room, attended by her mother, her mother-in-law, aunts and other women. Marshall was there, too. The rest of the men waited out of sight, smoke from their cigarettes drifting into the living room. She had two more children after that, both sons.

Today, at 50, Marshall looks like the epitome of a suburban dad. With his receding hairline, beard and broad physique, you could picture him browsing the aisles of The Home Depot. He possesses a gentle quality and doesn’t shy away from even harsh self-reflection.

The Followers abide by what they view as traditional gender roles, with men leading their households. Many male Followers work as contractors, electricians and plumbers; Marshall works as a consultant for a heating and air conditioning company. Women mostly focus on the home and their children. Jennifer cleans houses to supplement their income and homeschooled their kids for a time.

As a Follower, Marshall said he pressured his children to fit in at church. He believed the sect’s teachings about earning one’s way to salvation, and he spent many Sunday afternoons visiting the sick and caring for the dying. He and his wife never challenged the institution that shaped their lives.

articles.title: Prophecy, Scorn and a Rejection of This World: The Forbidding Vision of a Faith-Healing Preacher
articles.author: Noelle Crombie
paras: It was a stark and forbidding vision for those who followed the righteous path. Scorn, the preacher told his congregation, was a person’s lot if they led an “honest, clean, pure, godly life.” The world hated “people that live like that,” he said.
“They want you to be just as ungodly and filthy as they are,” he said in a rare audio recording, obtained by The Oregonian/OregonLive, of a 1958 sermon.

The preacher was Walter White, who led an Oregon City offshoot of the Followers of Christ, an Idaho sect that spurns medical treatment as a show of faith. White was a grocer, originally from Picabo, Idaho, whose congregants came to view as a prophet. He rambled at times during his sermon but always returned to simple and severe messages about choosing righteousness rather than the ways of the world. A trim figure in wire-rim glasses and dark combed-back hair, he spoke in a voice that evoked the stentorian tones of an old newsreel announcer. In the scratchy recording, people cough and babies cry as he preaches.

White was uneasy about being taped, according to a note by the congregant who made the recording. White didn’t want his message to fall into what he thought were undesirable hands. He viewed disbelievers with disgust. They put their trust in human experts, such as doctors, rather than in God. People like that, he told the faithful, “want to be somebody.” They want “the wisdom of the world and admiration.”

Today, nearly 60 years after White’s death, his pronouncements continue to influence the faithful. For many Followers, White remained “the highest authority,” said Mark Shaw, who left the sect in 2019 and keeps in touch with some Followers. Members invoked his teachings to settle disagreements. “It was used as the trump card,” he said. “It was the discussion-ender.”
To understand the modern-day Oregon City congregation, it’s essential to examine White’s role. No pastor ever succeeded him, leaving the sect all the more reliant on his teachings.

The Oregonian/OregonLive and ProPublica have published a series of articles in recent months about the Followers of Christ in Oregon and Idaho , focusing on the long history of parents in Followers congregations declining to seek medical care for their critically ill children and the sometimes fatal consequences .

Little has been publicly known about White, likely due to the Followers’ culture of isolation and secrecy. The Oregonian/OregonLive was able to piece together details through documents we obtained, including biographical sketches, a transcript and the recording of the sermon, along with written accounts of dreams White purported to have and records of baptisms he performed. Among the documents was a list of his prophecies and even a sex guide he disseminated.

White was born into the Followers, whose members migrated to Idaho from the Midwest around the turn of the 20th century. Men in White’s family preached, and he joined them in his 20s, the story goes, after he dreamed that worms would devour him if he didn’t.

In the early 1930s, White joined two church elders on a journey from Idaho to Oregon City to minister to a dying man. After talking with them, the man readily discarded his medications and was relieved to see White, an avid smoker, roll a cigarette because the man didn’t want to kick the habit. For the next five years, White traveled between Idaho and Oregon to preach and by 1938, he had moved to Oregon to lead a fledgling congregation.

Followers at the time were led by a constellation of preachers and elders, all men. Notes from one of their meetings in 1937 revealed that Followers believed White possessed the “gift of prophecy.” It also recorded the debates that simmered among them — whether women should be allowed to cut their hair, for instance. They talked about the value of dictionaries, which some classified as “worldly” items to be avoided, and determined that women assisting with home births should not “look under the cover” as women labored. One account written years later by a Follower suggested that White split with a prominent Idaho preacher after revelations that the man had sexual contact with a 15-year-old girl.

Some of those values still shape the Followers today. Congregants tend to stay out of what they view as the worldly affairs of politics and civic life, and they generally don’t pursue education beyond high school or vocational training. The Followers remain patriarchal; men are expected to lead their households.

White was known among Followers as “brother Walter.” An undated black-and-white photograph shows him baptizing a child in what appears to be a baptismal pool, his arm raised in prayer. In another image dated 1951, he wears a suit jacket and tie, a mug in one hand and a cigarette in the other.

As much a ruler as a spiritual leader, White enjoyed near-absolute authority. Followers believed he possessed such divine power that he knew their thoughts and secrets. They turned to him for approval on matters both consequential and mundane, from marital advice to appliance purchases. (White even weighed in on where to shop: He owned a local market and made it clear he expected to see Followers there.)

White’s earthly teachings extended to a perhaps unexpected realm: Couples on the cusp of marriage received a sex guide, which continued to be distributed as recently as 2018. Complete with explicit detail and anatomical diagrams, the 15-page manual includes chapters titled “the ideal love act” and “the control of climax.” And, in a seeming exception to the prohibition on medical treatment, it goes so far as to recommend that women who feel inhibited should consider seeing a doctor “who has given the sex problems sincere study.”

White preached the Oregon City sect’s singularity: His flock was spiritually superior to other Follower congregations, he contended, including ones in Idaho and Grants Pass, Oregon. By the 1950s, he had cut off ties to those groups.

In 1965, White told his congregation of his prophecy that the end times were near. He recounted a dream, which he said was set against the backdrop of the Kennedy Space Center in Florida, that involved walking with Jesus Christ, according to one account. He dreamed they climbed a launchpad, and White noted he was impressed with Christ’s physical agility. Days before White shared his vision, NASA launched Gemini 3, the first U.S. mission to send multiple astronauts into space.

White told the faithful that it was during this dream that Christ said the world would come to an end in six years. He said Christ warned that baptisms among the Followers would end even sooner. That his apocalyptic prophecy fizzled didn’t shake Followers’ faith.

White died in 1969. He was seen as irreplaceable. A handful of elders divided his leadership duties but lacked White’s authority. The faithful never tapped a successor, believing only a man called by God could fill the role. No one was ever deemed worthy enough to take his place.

But one element of White’s prophecy did come true. Given that he was the only person who could perform baptisms, his passing also meant that the ritual ended. As a result, the flock, which former members say numbered 1,500 or more at its peak, today consists solely of generations of the same families who were members in 1969.

Like other elders in the early days of the Followers, White saw illness as a test of faith. During the 1937 meeting, about 18 elders and preachers from congregations in Idaho and Oregon gathered at the Oregon City meetinghouse to settle the rules that would shape the church, according to a written account compiled by sect members years later.

The men discussed the Book of James in the New Testament, which says, “And the prayer of faith shall save the sick, and the Lord shall raise him up.” Followers interpret the lines as an edict to rely only on faith when faced with illness. The passage would be “strictly enforced to show faith,” according to an account of the meeting compiled years later. They believed that death, if it came, was God’s will.

Years later, in 1965, when the state investigated the case of a teen in the sect whose broken ankle had gone untreated, White said, “faith can heal,” according to a story in The Oregonian at the time. “We believe that God comes before man. If a person’s faith doesn’t go far enough, then he can seek help from man.”

The consequences of this belief system still reverberate. For years, the Oregon City Followers suffered multiple child deaths, many from treatable or preventable conditions. The deaths prompted the Legislature in 1999 to chip away at legal protections for parents whose children died without medical care. Then in 2011, lawmakers removed all protections for faith healing.

The faith-healing doctrine would affect White’s own descendants. Two of his great-granddaughters spent years in prison for failing to seek medical care for their premature newborns who died. In 2017, one of his great-great-granddaughters, Evelyn, suffered respiratory complications related to her premature birth. Authorities attribute her survival to the intervention of law enforcement officials who ordered her parents to get her to the hospital. Evelyn’s life and journey out of the Followers is the subject of a story and documentary published by The Oregonian/OregonLive and ProPublica.
The post Prophecy, Scorn and a Rejection of This World: The Forbidding Vision of a Faith-Healing Preacher appeared first on ProPublica .

articles.title: You likely have genes that affect how well your medications work – testing for them could improve treatment
articles.author:
<name>Philip Empey, Associate Professor, University of Pittsburgh School of Pharmacy, University of Pittsburgh</name>
      <foaf:homepage rdf:resource="https://theconversation.com/profiles/philip-empey-1455769"/>
paras: All people carry differences in their DNA that could affect how they respond to medication , according to my team’s newly published research. Moreover, 1 in 4 already take a medication their body processes differently because of their genetics.

Clinicians often take a trial and error approach to prescriptions. Two people take the same medicine at the same dose. One starts feeling better, but the other experiences side effects or sees little benefit. For some medications, part of the reason behind that difference in response is written in a person’s DNA.

The field of pharmacogenomics studies how variations in your DNA contribute to how your body processes and responds to medicines. For instance, genes can influence how quickly your liver breaks down a drug and how long it stays in your bloodstream.

But using genetic testing to guide prescriptions is not yet routine. Part of the problem is a lack of large population data to study this approach more broadly. Clinicians don’t know when it’s best to order genetic testing. And because most genetic research has been done on people of European ancestry , researchers know less about how common key gene variants are in everyone else.

To improve the diversity of pharmacogenomic data, my team of researchers and I analyzed the whole genome sequences and health records of nearly 100,000 participants in the All of Us Research Program . All of Us is an effort from the National Institutes of Health to study the health of 1 million or more people across the U.S. and its territories, with a focus on groups historically left out of biomedical research.

We examined 16 genes with well-established links to how someone responds to different medications, pairing this data with electronic health records to identify which drugs participants had already taken.

We found that every participant carried at least one relevant genetic variant , and many carried several. Around 99.5% of participants had a genetic variant for which the Food and Drug Administration or medical guidelines recommend a different drug or change in dose for certain medications.

Even more telling, about 24% had taken a drug that is affected by a genetic variant they carried. Common examples included drugs used to reduce excess stomach acid, such as omeprazole and pantoprazole, and statins used to lower cholesterol levels. Because health records can be incomplete, our results likely underestimate the actual prevalence of these gene-drug interactions.

These findings can help improve the databases clinicians and researchers use routinely in research. We identified 17,704 previously unreported variants in the regions of these genes that encode proteins. Computer models predicted that about a quarter may have significant effects on how the body processes drugs.
Our team also reported the frequencies of hundreds of genetic variants linked to drug response for people from genetic ancestries that previously had incomplete data.

Overall, our research shows that DNA variation is very common, and broader genetic testing may help optimize the medications clinicians prescribe to patients. It’s also an example of how big initiatives such as the All of Us Research Program can advance precision medicine .

However, this study doesn’t prove testing would improve outcomes for each of these people. Additionally, genes are only one factor; age, kidney and liver function, and other medications also affect how the body processes drugs .
Still, I believe the direction of the research is clear. Pharmacogenomics can provide potentially relevant benefits for many people who take medications.
Philip Empey receives funding from the NIH, Veterans Administration, Shear Family Foundation and Myers Family Foundation.

articles.title: The ‘religious left’ may be rising – but Black Christian women have been there all along
articles.author:
<name>Dara Delgado, Assistant Professor of Religion, University of North Carolina Wilmington</name>
      <foaf:homepage rdf:resource="https://theconversation.com/profiles/dara-delgado-1509269"/>
paras: During campaign season, headlines were full of candidates who spoke openly about their faith – and many of them were Democrats.

Adam Hamilton , the new senator-elect from Kansas, is pastor of the United States’ largest United Methodist congregation. Frederick Haynes , who will represent a Texas district in the U.S. House of Representatives, is a Baptist pastor. Texas Sen.-elect James Talarico is a Presbyterian seminary student who put a biblical commandment – “Love thy neighbor” – at the center of his campaign.

Since election night, journalists and commentators have attributed a significant amount of credit for the proverbial “Blue Wave” to the religious left . Although some mention Michigan Sen.-elect Abdul El-Sayed, who is Muslim, and Ohio Gov.-elect Amy Acton, who is Jewish, the focus has been on progressive Christians .

As a scholar of race, gender and religion whose work focuses on Black Protestant Christianity , I found post-election reporting about a rise in the religious left curious. Voters from many faith traditions did help power the “Blue Wave,” but one often-overlooked group has long been the left’s staunchest supporters: Black Christian women.

Focus on the “return” of the religious Democrats highlights the contrast between the religious diversity on the left and the allegiance between MAGA Republicans and evangelicals on the right . According to NBC exit polls , 82% of voters who consider themselves white evangelicals or born-again Christians voted for GOP candidates in 2026. In 2024, 82% of evangelicals in 10 key states voted for President Donald Trump .

But talking about religious Democrats as if they are a new, shiny bauble implies that, until this election, religious progressives have been off the ballot. That is simply not the case, especially when it comes to Black women.

Over the last four elections , majorities of both female voters and Black voters have voted blue . Black women vote for Democrats by an ever bigger margin : 93%, in 2026 exit polls, compared with 59% of women overall and 86% of Black men. Although Black women account for only 5-7% of Americans, they have been the most consistent Democratic voting bloc.

More than 7 in 10 Black Americans are Christian , and the vast majority are Protestant. Another 4% belong to other faiths, including Islam, and 22% are religiously unaffiliated. According to Pew’s 2023-24 Religious Landscape Survey , 2 in 3 members of Black Protestant denominations are women.
Many Black women candidates spoke about faith on the campaign trail.

For example, Keisha Lance Bottoms , the governor-elect of Georgia, attends a Methodist church . A few days after her victory, she spoke at the historic Ebenezer Baptist Church in Atlanta, pastored by Democratic Sen. Raphael Warnock of Georgia. During her visit, Lance Bottoms recalled that she had prayed about whether to run for governor and said that “God told me to go.” Her billionaire opponent was a “Goliath,” she said, but “ our God supplied all of our needs .”
Anita Earls , who was re-elected as a judge on the North Carolina Supreme Court, is a longtime member of the African Methodist Episcopal Church .

Among sitting Democrats, Delaware Sen. Lisa Blunt Rochester has spoken about her Christian faith . Massachusetts Rep. Ayanna Pressley , who grew up Baptist, has called herself “ a sister in Christ and a woman of faith. Someone who believes in the power of prayer.”
Each of these women is part of the religious left.

Before them was Shirley Chisholm , who became the first Black woman elected to Congress in 1968. Four years later, she was the first Black woman to run for president on the Democratic ticket. Her 1970 memoir, “ Unbought and Unbossed ,” recounts her commitment to progressive ideals, ranging from education to women’s reproductive rights, and to her Christian faith.

“America has the laws and the material resources it takes to ensure justice for all its people,” she wrote . “What it lacks is the heart, the humanity, the Christian love that it would take. It is perhaps unrealistic to hope that I can help give this nation any of those things, but that is what I believe I have to try to do.”

Before Black women were voted into office, however, they were already pillars of progressive politics . Historically, Black churches have been more than a place to foster belief. They have also been community-based institutions that fostered social, political and economic justice.

Within Black denominations, men tend to hold senior leadership positions. In his famed book “ The Souls of Black Folk ,” sociologist W.E.B. DuBois observed that the Black preacher was also a community “leader, a politician, an orator, a ‘boss,’ an intriguer, an idealist.”

Women’s role was less public, but no less vital , including social and political organizing. In “ Witnessing and Testifying ,” religion professor Rosetta Ross showed how Black women’s faith and activism inspired each other during the Civil Rights Movement. Among the women Ross surveyed is Ella Baker, who organized the initial meeting for what would become the Student Nonviolent Coordinating Committee and often “used Christian scripture to admonish listeners to fight” for freedom.

Women like Baker, voting rights activist Fannie Lou Hamer , and Clara Muhammad , wife of Nation of Islam founder Elijah Muhammad, show how Black communities’ concerns and faith often intertwined with progressive politics . In 1958, Nannie Helen Burroughs, founder of the Women’s Auxiliary of the National Baptist Convention , said that African American Christians wanted “ Jesus, jobs and justice .”
Today, too, faith guides many progressive Black women’s politics and public service. For voting rights activists, for example, casting a ballot is not just a right , but something sacred .

Over the past week, journalists and political pundits have drawn attention to the many different groups that moved to the left to fuel Democrats’ midterm victories, including young voters, Latinos, Asian Americans, men and political independents. Black women voters, meanwhile, have remained steady .

Indeed, history has shown how their steadiness helped guide the Democratic Party’s political and moral compass . And I am willing to wager that they will continue to play an essential role in what the left does between now and 2028.

Dara Delgado does not work for, consult, own shares in or receive funding from any company or organization that would benefit from this article, and has disclosed no relevant affiliations beyond their academic appointment.

articles.title: Seattle mayor lifts pause and will expand police surveillance cameras with new safeguards
articles.author: Kurt Schlosser
paras: Seattle will expand its police surveillance camera network to three more neighborhoods, Mayor Katie Wilson said Tuesday , ending a pause she put in place in March over privacy and civil liberties concerns.

The move comes a day after NYU’s Policing Project released an independent audit of the Seattle Police Department’s Real Time Crime Center (RTCC), which Wilson commissioned during the pause. The audit found the city had built “an important foundation” for overseeing the system but that “significant policy gaps remain.” It made 19 recommendations.

Cameras in the Stadium District, installed before this summer’s FIFA World Cup, will be turned on immediately, according to the mayor’s office. Cameras around Garfield High School and in the Capitol Hill nightlife district still need to be bought and installed, which will take months. The City Council approved all three areas in 2025.

Wilson briefly turned on the 22 stadium-area cameras during the World Cup, citing “credible threats” reported by law enforcement, and said they would go off after the tournament. The audit noted that police streamed live feeds throughout the event, despite a department policy against monitoring cameras without an active call or case.

“After reviewing the evidence, the recommendations, and the safeguards available to us, I believe there is an important and responsible role for the RTCC within Seattle’s public-safety system,” Wilson said in a statement.

Wilson said the city will adopt most of the audit’s recommendations. The police department will publish a public dashboard on how the crime center is used and tighten its rules on data retention, permissible uses and requests from outside agencies. A new advisory group will help write policies for privately owned cameras, protests and where future cameras go.

The Real Time Crime Center, which launched in 2025 , pulls live video from hundreds of cameras into a single command room at police headquarters. They include 303 police-owned cameras at 61 sites, 116 security cameras at police buildings, 96 city traffic cameras, and 23 cameras owned by three local businesses that share their feeds with police.

Analysts watch 911 calls as they come in and pull up nearby cameras to give officers details callers may have missed, such as what a suspect is wearing or which way they ran. They also comb through recorded footage to help detectives investigate past crimes. The system runs on Fusus, software from Axon, the Arizona-based maker of police body cameras and Tasers.

Police are barred from using facial recognition with the system. The software does include an AI tool that searches video for people, vehicles and other objects, but analysts told auditors they use it only as a last resort because it is unreliable. In one case, a search for a man in a gray top and gray pants returned an image of a pigeon.

Whether the system reduces crime remains an open question. The Seattle Police Department has said officers and detectives are three times more likely to make an arrest with help from crime center analysts, and that the center assisted in 17 homicide cases in 2025, helping close 10. But the audit notes that the department counts any analyst action as “support,” such as checking a camera, even if it produced nothing useful.

Broader research on crime centers is thin, the audit found, and studies of surveillance cameras on their own show mixed results. A University of Pennsylvania evaluation of Seattle’s program, commissioned by the city’s inspector general, isn’t expected until late 2027.

Critics have warned that footage could end up with federal immigration agents or out-of-state prosecutors pursuing people who come to Washington for abortions or gender-affirming care. The audit found that state and city laws limit such sharing, but they can’t fully prevent it. Outside agencies could still get footage through public records requests or court orders served on the city or on Axon, which stores some of the police department’s video in its cloud.

Tee Sannon, technology policy program director for the ACLU of Washington, said the group was “deeply disappointed” by the decision. With the audit having “reaffirmed significant gaps in privacy protections and accountability,” expanding the network “is a step in the wrong direction,” Sannon said. She added that the city should invest in proven alternatives such as community violence prevention programs.

“Used together, CCTV and RTCC supercharge law enforcement’s capabilities to monitor, track, and reconstruct people’s movements across the city,” Sannon said. Protecting residents, she said, requires strict, enforceable limits on how the technology is used, how long data is kept and who it’s shared with, along with independent oversight.

Wilson said the expansion and the new safeguards go together. “We can gather evidence to hold those who commit violent acts accountable and protect our neighbors targeted by federal overreach,” she said.

Business groups praised the decision. Jon Scholes, president and CEO of the Downtown Seattle Association, said the city “already has stringent privacy guardrails in place” and that, with police staffing “still lagging,” additional tools “are essential for solving crimes.” The Seattle Metro Chamber and Challenge Seattle, which have pushed the city to turn on the cameras, cited a poll they commissioned this year that found 75% of Seattle voters support using cameras to help active investigations.
“Residents and businesses have sent a clear message: they want our officers to have the tools to keep them safe,” said former Gov. Chris Gregoire, CEO of Challenge Seattle.

City Councilmember Bob Kettle, who chairs the council’s public safety committee, said the committee will take up the audit’s recommendations, along with those from the city’s inspector general and auditor.

The city also plans to lay groundwork for connecting cameras run by Seattle Center tenants and nearby businesses to the crime center, according to the mayor’s office, citing interest from those businesses after the Bite of Seattle shooting in July. The audit flagged private camera integration as a key area to watch: the police department has bought about 100 devices that let businesses stream video to the center but hasn’t decided who will get them.

The advisory group, which will include members of the Community Police Commission, the Community Surveillance Working Group, police and other city staff, will meet over the next few months. Its recommendations will then go through the police department’s policy review process.

articles.title: Microsoft awards $20K grants to 25 Seattle-area nonprofits amid state budget crunch and tax debate
articles.author: Todd Bishop
paras: The Lighthouse for the Blind is adding braille displays to its computer lab. Friends of the Issaquah Salmon Hatchery is taking its lessons to low-income schools. And Lake Washington High School’s band boosters are replacing marching capes that date to the MS-DOS era.

Those are among 25 King County nonprofits that received $20,000 apiece from Microsoft in grants announced this week. It’s the first round of the company’s Community-First Grants, a $1 million program launched in September .
Microsoft said it received 813 applications.

“Boy, I think we hit a nerve,” said Jane Broom, Microsoft’s senior director of Community Affairs, during an event Monday recognizing the nonprofits on the company’s Redmond campus, featuring Mariners catcher Cal Raleigh and the team’s mascots.

The grants are meant for immediate needs, such as replacing a broken-down van or a failed freezer, Broom explained. Nonprofits that already received or were invited to receive Microsoft corporate grants in 2026 weren’t eligible.

Funding and the tax debate: Nonprofits are dealing with rising costs and tighter budgets. As a group, their largest funding source is the state government, which is in the middle of an ongoing debate with members of the business community over taxes and economic competitiveness amid a budget crunch.

Microsoft is among the companies asserting that current and proposed taxes are hurting the business climate. It’s also the second-largest funder of the state’s nonprofits, behind only the state itself, said Brad Smith, the company’s president and vice chair.

“In my view, a healthy nonprofit community actually has aspects of support from more than one source,” Smith said in an interview after the event, noting that state grants are often at risk when a recession forces budget cuts.

Where the money goes: Demand is climbing for many of the grant recipients. At Community Lunch on Capitol Hill , which serves free hot meals, it’s up 40% this year, and the diaper bank at Byrd Barr Place has grown from 720 families in 2021 to 1,600, Microsoft said at the event.

Friends of the Issaquah Salmon Hatchery gives more than 700 tours during the salmon season. It will use its grant to bring lessons to classrooms, mainly at Title I schools, which serve large numbers of low-income students and often can’t afford a field trip to the hatchery, said Mark Clemens, the group’s executive director.

“If they can’t bring the school to the hatchery, we will go out to the school,” said Clemens, a former Scientific American art director, who was creative director of the Modernist Cuisine cookbook project before taking over the nonprofit in 2023.

One bonus for the group, which goes by the clever acronym of FISH, was the appearance of the Mariners’ salmon mascots, which joined the group onstage for a photo op when Clemens and his colleagues accepted its grant.

The Lighthouse for the Blind, a Seattle-based nonprofit that employs blind people in manufacturing, retail and other jobs, will use its grant to upgrade its computer training lab with Windows 11 PCs, braille displays and wireless keyboards, said Antonio Rozier, the nonprofit’s IT director.

The goal is to keep employees current on screen readers and other tools so they can work alongside sighted colleagues, Rozier said. The Lighthouse also has computer labs at its three manufacturing plants, and employees can use them for personal tasks, since some don’t have that equipment at home.
Rozier called the upgraded lab “a game changer for the future.”
The Lake Washington High School Band and Jazz Boosters will buy 150 uniforms for the school’s marching band, which returned in 2025 after a 40-year absence and has been performing in capes from 1981.

Microsoft’s company culture: Most of the company’s local giving is directed by its employees. Microsoft matches their donations and adds $25 for every hour they volunteer, up to a combined $15,000 a year per person, Smith said.
That program accounts for most of the $1.9 billion that Microsoft and its employees have given to about 13,000 Washington nonprofits over the past 30 years, he said.
“We let our people decide where the money goes,” Smith said.

Microsoft’s employee base is going through a period of major change. After layoffs in July and September , the company offered voluntary buyouts last month to about 60,000 people, roughly a quarter of its global workforce. Employees have described mounting pressure to use AI, stagnant pay and a growing sense of job insecurity, The New York Times reported .
Asked about the buyouts, Smith said it’s a good time for Microsoft to keep investing in the employee experience, and he described the giving program as part of that.

Silicon Valley companies may offer more free food as a perk, he said, but Microsoft matches employee donations, giving workers who often move to the region from elsewhere a way to get involved in the community.

This year’s Microsoft Give campaign in October, the company’s biggest month for employee donations, was again a success, Smith said, showing that “employee participation and employee giving is alive and well.”
Microsoft plans to open a second round of applications for the Community-First Grants in the spring of 2027.

articles.title: King County Metro planning service changes for new Renton Transit Center
articles.author: Alex Kvenvolden
paras: As part of the Stride S1 line, Sound Transit is building a new transit center in Renton, adjacent to the existing South Renton Park and Ride. When it opens in 2028, it will be known as simply Renton Transit Center, and will replace both the existing Renton Transit Center in downtown Renton, and the adjacent South Renton Park and Ride. Commuters need not fret over lack of parking, as the new transit center will include a new garage dedicated for commuter parking that is larger than the parking at both current facilities that are reserved for transit commuters. With the transit center moving, bus service has to move with it, and Metro has made its first service proposal on what that may look like in its Renton Area Mobility Project (RAMP). Details below the jump.

King County Metro is proposing moving every route that serves the current Renton Transit Center in downtown Renton to the future Renton Transit Center. Multiple services (including both RapidRide lines) will continue to downtown Renton, but the relocated transit center will be the new transfer hub for all routes.

To move the connection point, routes 148 and 153 (which already serve the South Renton P&R before continuing to the current transit center) are going to be shortened to the new transit center (and not continue downtown). Routes 105, 240, and 907 are going to be lengthened further south to reach the new transit center. Routes 106 and 107 are going to be redirected away from downtown to the new transit center, and routes 101, 102, RapidRides F and I (current 160) lines are seeing no substantial change in routing.

Additionally, route 153 will move to operate on SW 7th St to Lind Ave in both directions, and the RapidRide F Line will move off of SW 7th, Lind Ave, and SW 16th St to run on SW Grady Way from the new Renton Transit Center to Oaksdale Ave SW. Lastly, the two Metro Flex zones serving the existing transit center will be adjusted to both cover the relocated transit center.

Service levels across most routes are going to be the same, but there are some exceptions. The most welcome change in my opinion is that route 907 will be expanded to start earlier and run later (6am to 6pm). Currently, the 907 doesn’t serve peak direction commutes at all, because historically these were covered by route 143 (e.g., northbound trips in the morning peak were all 143 trips, and after the commute is done, route 907 would start running). As a result, the last trip of the “night” on route 907 to Black Diamond from Renton TC leaves at 3:45pm (because route 143 would start covering that trip shortly after that). However, route 143 is still suspended, as it has been since 2020. Metro’s proposal will finally delete route 143 about 8 years after it was suspended, with the freed up service hours being used to expand service on route 907 and to implement the rest of the plan.

One other change in service is that short route 102 trips (which are ones that go from Seattle to S. Renton P&R, but not to Fairwood) will be converted to route 101. The same number of trips will run from Seattle to both Renton and Fairwood, but service will be simplified so that all 102 trips go to Renton TC and Fairwood, and all 101 trips will go to Renton TC and downtown Renton.

While the plan does a decent job at connecting current service to the Stride station at the new transit center, it does not provide any connections to the other Stride station in Renton at NE 44th St. I think this is a particularly unfortunate omission because parking at this station was delayed to the mid 2030s in the first realignment plan, meaning that for its first several years, the NE 44th St Station will only be useful for people going to or from walking distance of the station itself. A bus route connecting the station to the frequent route 240 a couple miles east could give local residents a way to access nearby Stride service, but as it stands, Stride service at NE 44th will be completely unusable for many local residents until the parking garage is completed.
I asked King County Metro if they had considered adding connections to NE 44th St, including a concept route that is part of their Metro Connects interim map, and I got this response:

The implementation of a new route to serve this station was not part of the scope of the Renton Area Mobility Project. As a budget-constrained project, the focus is on trying to facilitate the transit center relocation (which would require more operating resources than on the ground today, as more routes need to be extended to the new facility than there are routes that can be truncated at the new facility), without a reduction to current service levels. That task alone was challenging, and there unfortunately isn’t remaining project budget to pursue service growth at the scale of implementing a new route like [the route from Metro Connects].

While it is probably the correct decision to keep this particular project narrowly focused on the area around downtown Renton due to how many routes need to be changed in this one area and the limited amount of service hours to work with, I do hope Metro is able to secure more funding for the other station in the near future, and will evaluate potential service options whether or not they can budget additional service hours.

When I first got familiar with route 101, it was different than today. Rather than starting at South Renton P&R, then going to Renton TC, then Seattle, it actually did the Renton area “backwards”, by starting at Renton TC, then going south a bit to South Renton P&R, then going to Seattle. I always thought this was odd, because Renton TC was clearly the dominant transit hub, and also because it was going to the south park and ride before heading back north.

With south Renton being the transit hub starting in 2028, I think it makes sense to bring back the “backwards” route 101. It will save transferring riders about 10 minutes on each trip, which is quite significant!
If you have any thoughts on the proposal, sound off below, and be sure to take Metro’s survey by November 30.

articles.title: WSDOT Seeks Feedback in I-5 High Speed Rail Survey
articles.author: Doug Trumm
paras: State officials are trying to keep the dream alive of high speed rail connecting the Cascadia region and linking Seattle, Portland, and Vancouver. The Washington State Department of Transportation (WSDOT) has a public survey open through November 13.

The survey will refine high speed rail options while also shaping the I-5 master plan the agency is putting together at the same time. Yoking together the planning for the region's primary freeway and its most promising HSR route was a conscious decision on WSDOT's part, aiming to underscore the crash course the region is on toward transportation gridlock – at least without significant intervention.

"The Cascadia megaregion is expected to grow by 3.4 million more people by 2050. This growth is equivalent to adding a city almost the size of Los Angeles to the megaregion," WSDOT noted on its project page . "The increase in population will be matched by economic growth across industries like technology, aerospace, healthcare and logistics. Recent studies show that the strain on our existing transportation system will be significant by 2050."

The survey does not provide much new information for folks who have already been engaged in this high speed rail process, which WSDOT has long been exploring – going back to a 2017 feasibility study , a 2019 business case study , and a 2020 framework study outlining a path to cross-border governmental collaboration.
WSDOT did share a project definition that sets a goal of achieving top speeds of at least 160 miles per hour.

"The purpose of the Cascadia High-Speed Rail project is to provide reliable high-speed rail service at speeds greater than 160 mph or 260 kph that is competitive with other transportation modes and improves mobility between the Cascadia megaregion’s metropolitan areas. The project purpose includes optimizing the safe and efficient movement of people in the growing Cascadia megaregion and facilitating economic development."

According to a presentation from September at the Washington Transportation Commission, the high speed rail program is spending the next year identifying "potentially feasible" route options, before spending another year refining those options.

"The Service Development Plan will be an analysis of potential routes where high speed rail could operate, an analysis of conceptual service options like the number of train trips and the number of stops that a high speed service may have," Ben Tripousis, WSDOT's Cascadia High-Speed Rail and I-5 Program Administrator told the commission. "We'll look at financing and governance as a component of the service development plan development. What the service development plan will not determine is a preferred route option or specific station locations at this time. That will be accomplished in future analysis."

WSDOT clarified that HSR would be a complement rather than a replacement for existing Amtrak Cascades service: "Cascadia High-Speed Rail would complement the existing Amtrak Cascades passenger rail service. High-speed rail would make fewer stops and travel at greater speeds than conventional rail services, likely running on new, dedicated tracks. Think of high-speed rail as the express train, while Amtrak Cascades would be the local route."

WSDOT is leading on the planning effort because 277 of the 315 miles between Portland and Vancouver, B.C. are in Washington state. That stretch could be spanned in as little as two hours with high speed rail, depending on the number of stops and the maximum speeds achieved.
In the final days of the Biden Administration, WSDOT secured a $49.7 million federal grant to fund the creation a service development plan for Cascadia high-speed rail.

WSDOT will likely be facing pressure from some quarters to widen I-5 in its master plan process. Former WSDOT secretary Roger Millar warned that widening I-5 would be prohibitively expansive and ineffective, since car traffic would swell to clog the wider artery.

High speed rail would be pricey in its own right, but with much better ability to scale up and solve the underlying problem. Unlike adding another freeway lane on I-5, high-speed rail can boost frequency to meet increased demand, rather than quickly succumbing to congestion issues and getting trapped in a cycle of induced demand .

Whether freeway expansions or light rail , large infrastructure projects are facing massive increases in construction costs, which is sure to impact high-speed rail projects as well. These cost increases are tied to a period of high inflation and sky-high costs on construction materials (linked to Trump tariffs) and fuel (tied to Trump's war in Iran). In its 2017 study, WSDOT estimated Cascadia “ultra-high speed rail” would cost between $24 billion and $42 billion — and that was before the era of high construction cost escalation hit.
A higher price tag is running headlong into a period of retreating public investment in passenger rail.

Republicans have also been pushing to overhaul grant programs funded in Biden's Infrastructure and Jobs Act to punish transit projects. Now that Democrats have retaken control of Congress, gutting transit investment seemingly should be off the agenda – although some Democrats like Washington's own Rep. Rick Larsen (who is the frontrunner to secure the coveted position of House transportation committee chair) had signed on the Republican-led legislation, which has an Orwellian name: the BUILD America 250 Act.

Meanwhile, some rail advocates have argued high speed rail has boondoggle potential – pointing to the over budget and very behind schedule California high speed rail project – as they push the state should prioritize more incremental improvements to Amtrak Cascades service that could be achieved sooner. Studies have shown high demand for conventional rail that could easily support doubling Cascades frequencies to 16 daily trips – which state lawmakers affirmed as a goal without yet allocating funding to make it happen.

Since the state is envisioning high speed rail as an express service serving fewer stops, more frequent "local" Cascades service would serve a valuable purpose once the bullet train arrives, feeding the high speed hub stations and keeping the in-between cities connected. And in the interim, it would build up a base of ridership so high speed rail can hit the ground running.

State officials are aiming to complete the high speed rail service development plan by 2028. That may put the region in position to win federal funding from a new federal administration more friendly to transit than Trump has been.

Since high speed rail will likely take more than a decade to build, its success may also require a period of political stability and continued federal commitment to infrastructure investment that the United States has not seen over the last decade. But the 2026 midterm could potentially portend a larger political shift – at least if that momentum can be sustained and cultivated.
Complete WSDOT's survey by Friday, November 13.

articles.title: GLP-1 drugs carry risk of rare but serious eye condition – a physician studying these medicines explains the potential side effect
articles.author:
<name>Ziyad Al-Aly, Clinical Epidemiologist, Washington University in St. Louis</name>
      <foaf:homepage rdf:resource="https://theconversation.com/profiles/ziyad-al-aly-513663"/>
paras: GLP-1 drugs must now carry a warning label about a potential link to a rare eye condition that can result in vision loss, the U.S. Food and Drug Administration announced on Nov. 9. 2026. The eye condition is called non-arteritic anterior ischemic optic neuropathy , or NAION, and doctors often refer to it as a stroke of the eye.
I am a clinician and epidemiologist who has studied GLP-1 drugs, and my colleagues and I published one of the studies that identified a link between GLP-1 drugs and NAION .

Millions of people around the world take these medications – including 30 million in the U.S. – to treat diabetes and obesity and reduce the risk of cardiovascular disease. They are also being investigated for an expanding list of clinical conditions .

The data on which the FDA’s warning is based suggests a real but low risk of NAION for people taking GLP-1 medications. This is not a trivial or inconsequential outcome for those who develop the eye stroke. But on balance, if you’re using the medication for an FDA-approved condition such as diabetes or obesity on the advice of your doctor, the risk should not deter you from doing so.
Here’s what patients who use GLP-1 drugs need to know about this rare but serious side effect.

NAION is an injury to the optic nerve , which is the nerve that connects the eye to the brain. This eye condition is caused by a sudden reduction in blood flow. Without enough blood flow, patients may experience sudden, painless blurry vision, dark patches, partial loss of vision or even blindness.

These symptoms generally persist and often lead to permanent visual impairment. Patients often notice these symptoms first thing in the morning when they wake up, as it tends to happen more frequently at night when blood pressure is naturally lower.

As use of GLP-1 drugs increased – particularly since 2021, when they were approved for obesity – cases of NAION began to emerge. A 2024 study of close to 17,000 patients referred to ophthalmology clinics was the first to show a potential link. It reported an increased risk of the eye condition among the subset of those patients who were prescribed a GLP-1 drug.

To determine that the connection was strong enough to merit a warning, the FDA first compiled data from 126 randomized, controlled clinical trials of GLP-1 drugs. Those trials included a total of 134,253 patients – 78,217 of them were on GLP-1 drugs and 56,036 received a placebo or a different medication, for comparison.

Per year, on average, the incidence of NAION cases was 6.4 per 100,000 people for patients taking the GLP-1 drugs and 3.8 per 100,000 among people given a placebo or other drug. This translated into 2.6 extra cases of NAION per 100,000 patients on GLP-1 drugs.

In a separate analysis, the FDA reviewed GLP-1 drug data from its own network of sentinel programs that track the real-world safety of approved medications. They assessed how often people with type 2 diabetes who started either a GLP-1 drug or two other common types of diabetes medications reported having NAION between 2019 and 2024.

Patients taking GLP-1 drugs had a small but meaningfully higher risk compared to one type of diabetes drug, called DPP-4 inhibitors, which prevent the breakdown of the body’s own natural GLP-1. Over the course of one year, those taking GLP-1 drugs experienced NAION at a rate of 32 per 100,000 and those taking DPP-4 inhibitors at a rate of 26 per 100,000. This resulted in 6 extra cases of NAION per 100,000 patients among people on GLP-1 drugs.

Other studies that use real-world data such as electronic health records or insurance claims to track the health of people over many years have also found a consistent association between GLP-1 drugs and NAION .

For example, my colleagues and I tracked nearly 600,000 U.S. veterans with type 2 diabetes starting either a GLP-1 drug or a different drug over three years. For patients on GLP-1 drugs, we found that the incidence of this eye disorder was roughly 390 cases per 100,000 people, compared with 290 per 100,000 on an alternative medication. In other words, among people taking GLP-1 drugs, there were about 100 extra cases per 100,000 patients.

That number varied somewhat across studies, probably because of group differences among patients. For example, in some, patients were on average older, or also had other conditions that might contribute to their risk.

What’s clear is that the slightly increased risk of NAION does not seem to be specific to any one GLP-1 drug but can occur regardless of which GLP-1 drug a patient takes. It’s possible that some GLP-1 drugs may have a higher risk than others, but so far, there’s no research addressing this.

The FDA’s announcement follows a 2025 review by European regulators, which examined NAION risk in only one type of GLP-1 drug, called semaglutide. It concluded that this eye condition is a very rare side effect of semaglutide and mandated that the package insert be updated to include NAION as a very rare side effect.

The risk of NAION with GLP-1 drugs is likely real. All the evidence – the FDA’s two analyses, the real-world studies conducted by independent researchers and the fact that two regulators reached the same view independently – points in the same direction.

But in terms of the total number of people who are likely to experience this side effect, the risk is small. In my view, this makes the FDA’s warning not a cause for alarm but rather an unlikely but not impossible outcome that both clinicians and patients should be aware of.
Clinicians should discuss it with their patients before prescribing a GLP-1 drug – and patients should be educated on the symptoms of NAION and how to tell if they are experiencing it.

Patients should also seek immediate care at the earliest signs of vision problems. For patients who have previously had NAION or who already have risk factors for it , including smoking, diabetes, high blood pressure, sleep apnea, anemia and kidney disease, careful discussion weighing the risks and benefits is important.

articles.title: Pa. Gov. Josh Shapiro’s popularity and ‘get sh-t done’ attitude might not cut it in crowded 2028 Democratic field – but he has options
articles.author:
<name>Alison Dagnes, Professor of Political & Social Inquiry, Shippensburg University</name>
      <foaf:homepage rdf:resource="https://theconversation.com/profiles/alison-dagnes-2775931"/>
paras: The 2026 midterm elections swept Democrats into office around the country in such numbers that journalists were running out of synonyms for “ massive .”

In Pennsylvania, Gov. Josh Shapiro won reelection by 22 percentage points, winning more than 60% of the vote – something that has been accomplished only twice before in the modern era in the Keystone State.

Not only did Shapiro wipe the floor with his opponent Stacy Garrity, the state treasurer, but he also helped flip four U.S. House seats from red to blue. His coattails benefited down-ballot candidates , helping Democrats solidify their control of the state House and flip the state Senate as well .
Shapiro’s political stock in Pennsylvania is riding high.

I’m a political science professor and political media researcher in central Pennsylvania, and many of my former students work in Harrisburg. Some are Democrats working for or around the governor; others are Republicans working in different corners of state government. All are finely tuned to the political gossip that swirls around a successful politician whose star is on the rise. It is the worst-kept secret in American politics that Josh Shapiro wants to be president.

I’ve met the governor a handful of times and can attest to his George Clooney-level charisma. He’s a hard worker, has maintained a remarkably clean political profile, and is from many accounts a genuinely nice dude.
And yet, there are plenty of reasons his ambitions may require some careful timing, regardless of his personal strengths.

Shapiro’s political victories didn’t just happen. Over the past four years, he has worked to demonstrate bipartisan competence as Pennsylvania’s chief executive, adopting an expression he uses frequently: “ get sh-t done .”
Now, with Democrats holding the governor’s office and both chambers of the General Assembly, Shapiro told reporters : “We got the power now, the House, the Senate. We have to deliver.”

Shapiro’s approval ratings have remained strong , consistent with his reelection margins. That’s unusual in a state that has swung back and forth between supporting Donald Trump in 2016 , Joe Biden in 2020 and Trump again in 2024 , each time by fewer than 2 percentage points.
If Shapiro is indeed seriously eyeing the White House , his current popularity will certainly serve him well. But winning the presidency is an enormous undertaking, particularly in a crowded field.

With Trump unable to run in 2028, the next presidential election will feature open seats for both parties and likely attract many candidates. Democrats, in particular, have a deep bench of attractive potential contenders .

There are so many possibilities that Shapiro could find himself running against people very much like him: younger centrists, swing-state politicians and accomplished elected officials with solid records. Consider just a few names that could be part of the conversation: Georgia Sen. Jon Ossoff, Illinois Gov. JB Pritzker and former Chicago Mayor Rahm Emanuel.

Shapiro would have to find a way to distinguish himself in a field filled with candidates who can make many of the same arguments about their experience, political appeal and accomplishments. That’s a tall order. A Plan B might be wise.
Fortunately for Shapiro, other choices abound.

He could run for the Senate in 2028 against incumbent John Fetterman, if Fetterman seeks reelection . This would be a twofer: Shapiro would continue his rise in politics, and he would likely beat a guy he apparently does not like. The two reportedly don’t speak , much less get along.

Shapiro could also position himself for a vice presidential nomination by attaching himself to another 2028 hopeful. This would buy him time to build his national profile, allow the presidential field to sort itself out and potentially put him in a strong position for another run at the White House down the road. It would also give him an opportunity to demonstrate that he can work effectively on a national stage.

Or he could angle for a Cabinet post. The federal government has undergone significant restructuring under DOGE and Trump’s executive orders. Should a Democrat win the White House in 2028, rebuilding federal agencies and restoring institutional capacity will be a monumental undertaking. Shapiro could be an attractive candidate for a major administrative role.

The bottom line for Shapiro is that he will need to distinguish himself from a crowded field of Democrats by emphasizing his statewide victories in a major swing state, impressive fundraising ability and a political voice that can evoke Barack Obama without alienating either his party or the broader electorate. That’s a tricky feat, even for the most talented politicians.

But Nov. 3, 2026, showed us that he knows how to make sh-t happen. Whatever he decides, the next two years will be important for Shapiro, consequential for Democrats, and fascinating for political scientists like me, who will be watching events unfold with a keen eye and, probably, a bucket of popcorn.
Read more of our stories about Philadelphia and Pennsylvania , or sign up for our Philadelphia newsletter on Substack .
