articles.title: Students creating documentaries with scientists deepens STEM belonging and public trust in science
articles.author:
<name>Dena K. Seidel, Science Communication Researcher and Science Filmmaker, Rutgers University</name>
      <foaf:homepage rdf:resource="https://theconversation.com/profiles/dena-k-seidel-2508952"/>
paras: Marine scientists navigate autonomous glider robots across the Atlantic Ocean and along the West Antarctic Peninsula , collecting data to help predict storm intensity.
When farmers’ fields are destroyed by an unknown pathogen, plant scientists spend years breeding new varieties of disease-resistant food crops.
A team of microbiologists explore deep-sea volcanoes in search of organisms that may contain anticancer compounds.

These are passionate people who are dedicated to seeking solutions to real-world problems. They are also the main characters in science documentaries produced in the Rutgers Immersive Learning Science Storytelling Lab that I oversee. Our lab pairs students with working scientists to co-create documentaries about research as it happens, while earning experiential learning credit.
At a time when confidence in science is declining , I was approached by scientists who wanted their authentic research stories communicated to broad audiences.

I am an educator, a researcher and anthropologist , and a science filmmaker who has been making science documentaries with Rutgers students and researchers since 2008. The science-in-action storytelling model I developed is intended to make the human journey of science visible to the public. Our stories communicate the process, motivations and integrity behind science, which helps earn public confidence and trust in science .

I also partner with STEM learning researchers to gauge whether our documentaries increase the relatability of scientists, increase public understanding of scientific processes and help students find belonging in STEM.
Science-in-action storytelling is composed of five steps that support student-scientist relationships.
First, the storytellers develop trust with the participating university scientists. This trust stems from shared respect and a mutual understanding of the co-creation process.
The scientists then invite storytellers into their labs and field sites, where we capture their research processes in real time. This is Step 2.

Our professional storytelling team, which includes students, then documents scientists conducting research, including experiments and data collection, as they describe the why and how of their work. Depending on the complexity of the project, we collect dozens to hundreds of hours of science-in-action video footage.

Importantly, this video data is maintained in our storytelling lab, as it often includes recordings of federally funded research. Maintaining the video data repository is a key component to establishing and sustaining trust with the participating scientists.

Step 3 invites students to immerse themselves in the video data and begin shaping the footage into documentary scenes, constructed using only the scientists’ words, without narration. As they analyze hours of footage, our students learn about the authentic scientific processes; in doing so, they participate in research through the process of storytelling.
Our students are not graded on their documentary skills, nor are they required to make a film. Instead, they are graded on the science they learn through the storytelling process.

Step 4 requires that the students share drafts of their documentary scenes with the featured scientist to verify the accuracy of the science communicated. This step is part of the foundational trust agreement with the scientists but is also an opportunity for the students to personally connect with scientists.

For Step 5, our lab works to distribute the documentaries to a wide variety of audiences, including the general public. Here we partner with STEM learning experts to assess audiences’ understanding of and trust in the science communicated in the film and audience perceptions of the featured scientists.

Our completed science-in-action documentaries have reached audiences far beyond the university. Our National Science Foundation-funded “ Antarctic Edge: 70° South ” had a theatrical release and aired on Netflix. “ Atlantic Crossing ” was broadcast on PBS stations and was included in a three-year Smithsonian exhibit . “ Fields of Devotion ” was shared by the Association of American Universities as part of its campaign to increase public trust in science . And our lab’s newest long-form documentary, “ Mysteries of 9° North ,” co-created with 14 undergraduates and featuring scientists studying life at deep-sea volcanoes, will be released to the public in early 2027.

Our surveys capture how these science documentaries change audience understanding of science and how it is done. For example, after screening “ Antarctic Edge ,” viewers’ self-reported understanding of climate change rose from 71% to 91% . On a 15-item knowledge quiz, average scores rose, with gains of up to 24 percentage points on the concepts they knew least about.

When 102 undergraduates were asked what made the scientists in “ Fields of Devotion ” relatable, they named passion for the subject (72%), desire to help others (71%) and commitment to their work (70%).

Our survey results also suggest that students who participated in the lab gained confidence and feelings of belonging in a science community. Undergraduates who once said they did not feel “smart enough” reported that they could now see themselves as scientists . All participating students reported that their collaboration with scientists positively transformed their understanding of science.
Nonscience majors gained a deep understanding of the scientific process, while science majors gained rare access to research outside their own disciplines.

Student-directed science documentaries include “ Growing the Caribbean Glider Fleet ,” featuring scientists monitoring hurricane development; “ Biting Back: The Lifesaving Potential of Catnip ,” about the development of natural insect repellents; “ Where Waters Meet on the Breathing Shore ,” featuring climate scientists studying coastal ecosystems; “ The B.A.S.I.L Project ,” about USDA-funded plant-breeding research; “ Ocean Farming ,” about NOAA supported oyster breeding; “ The Women of Nsongwe ,” about USAID-supported agriculture projects in Zambia; and “ Skycatcher ,” about an NSF-funded atmospheric chemistry study in Alabama.

This science-in-action model offers a path forward that other universities could follow. Institutions can strengthen students’ STEM learning and science identities while training a new generation of credible, relatable voices for science.
Uncommon Courses is an occasional series from The Conversation U.S. highlighting unconventional approaches to teaching.

articles.title: Democrats’ agenda will be set by their ability to organize and compromise — not by the socialist, progressive or centrist factions all claiming victory
articles.author:
<name>SoRelle Wyckoff Gaynor, Assistant Professor of Public Policy and Politics, University of Virginia</name>
      <foaf:homepage rdf:resource="https://theconversation.com/profiles/sorelle-wyckoff-gaynor-2532648"/>
paras: The massive Democratic majority in the U.S. House and Senate that was ushered in by a historic blue midterm vote is an ideologically diverse one .

Candidates spent much of the past year differentiating their positions from the mainstream Democratic coalition. The result is a freshman class filled with as many progressive liberals as moderate problem solvers .

By the morning after Election Day, pundits and current Democratic members across the political spectrum were quick to claim their ideologically aligned candidates as the “ majority makers ” – the group most responsible for the large victory.
Centrist Democrats pointed to pragmatic moderates flipping Trump-won seats. Liberal voices highlighted the enthusiasm and turnout driven by a new, progressive vision.
As a result, days after the election the focus had turned toward January: Who will become the majority maker within Congress?

Party caucus leaders have already started building their roster : The Progressive Caucus claims at least 25 new members in their ranks, growing their membership to over 100 Democratic members. The moderate Blue Dog Caucus doubled in size , from 10 to 20 new members. And in the middle, the center-left New Dems are projecting a caucus of over 140 members.

I’m a political scientist who has worked in and now studies Congress . Figuring out the dynamics and direction of the 120th Congress requires looking at more than the ideological positions of the candidates who won. Instead, focusing on the number of candidates who won can provide insight into the direction of the party as a whole.

The large – and at the time of writing, still growing – margins of Democratic control in the 120th Congress are the biggest since 1993 , before Congress became consistently competitive and increasingly polarized. Those large margins provide essential context for understanding how this new ideological coalition will work in Congress.

While history demonstrates that an ideologically diverse party can be hard to wrangle , the size of the new Democratic majority provides some breathing room for policy negotiation and procedural debates.

Unlike the current Republican Caucus that is reliant on keeping historically narrow majorities together to pass party goals, future Democratic leadership can stand to lose a few votes. With a minimum of 254 seats in the House and 54 seats in the Senate , small-scale Democratic defections are irrelevant.
This breathing room provides the potential for negotiation, while also limiting any mandate an ideological group may claim.

For instance, the 120th Congress will have eight members in the House who are backed or affiliated with the Democratic Socialists of America , known as the DSA. In raw terms of political power, when the majority has at least 36 votes to spare on any given party-line bill, this group may not matter in policymaking.

If a group – say, the entirety of the Progressive Caucus’ 100-plus membership – decides to stick together, leadership will be forced to listen. Thus, the potential power of ideological factions depends not only on their ideas but their own organizational skills.

When groups in Congress develop practices such as confidential meetings or binding rules that require members vote together on certain votes, the legitimacy of group demands can be strengthened. This is a strategy that has been employed with relative success by the far-right Republican Freedom Caucus since it was formed in 2014.
The overarching policy goals for newly elected Democrats are consistent across the ideological spectrum: lowering the cost of living and rooting out corruption.

This was highlighted in acceptance speeches by Democrats from South Carolina to Texas to Michigan . All emphasized the same policy-focused promise: Instead of fighting left versus right, the fight should focus on the top versus the bottom.
This shared vision is no doubt important. My research has shown that a cohesive message is a key part of winning and maintaining majority control.

However, the “blue tsunami” was powered by voters with very specific policy demands. And as is always the case with policymaking, the details matter. Does healthcare reform mean reinstating the Obamacare subsidies set to expire on Jan. 1, 2027? Or does it mean something bolder, such as Medicare for All ?
While there is power in numbers, the organizational strength and ultimate success of ideological groups in Congress depends on how unified they can be around specific policy goals and proposals.
This means that who is doing the unifying also matters.
The success of any potential legislative package heavily relies on congressional leaders’ knowledge of congressional rules and their willingness to incorporate member viewpoints.

This necessity of having leadership in place to get legislation moving is epitomized by the order of operations for a new congressional session. In the coming weeks, both parties will hold closed-door, secret-ballot elections to select their new party leaders . That’s well before any legislation is even drafted.

With a Democratic caucus filled with anti-establishment candidates across the ideological spectrum, and external pressure from political pundits to dump current Democratic leadership , the future of the Democratic Party has been projected onto this otherwise ritualistic vote .

But the power and success of congressional leadership lies in its procedural acumen, not its ideological vision. Some already in Congress have noted New York Democratic Rep. Hakeem Jeffries’ experience and working relationships in discussions of whether he should be house speaker. Furthermore, groups can extract concessions during leadership selection in exchange for their support, such as seats on powerful committees or an agreement on policy agenda items.

Sen. Chuck Schumer, the longtime New York lawmaker aiming to lead Senate Democrats again, faces more public criticism from his party . While no one has yet stepped up as an alternative, momentum is building for Maryland Sen. Chris Van Hollen , who has said he is “in listening mode.”

To external observers, the selection of party leadership seems like a defining point for the party. But whether a new caucus translates to new leaders or new rules ultimately depends on the organizational power of new members and their already-serving co-workers – and what a party leader can offer them in terms of policy goals and procedural capabilities. Who is chosen as leader is not necessarily a signal of what the party’s policy goals will be.

That picture is not yet clear – and it may not be for some time. After all, the new Democratic margins in Congress are a result of a collection of majority makers. The margins of victory tell a story about more than presidential backlash. Across the country, progressive enthusiasm and moderate appeal turned voters toward the Democratic Party . And while everything is local, national enthusiasm matters, too.

The 120th Congress will include progressives and moderates and the establishment candidates in the middle that are all required parts of the same whole. Or as political scientist E.E. Schattschneider argued in 1960 in his seminal work “ The Semisovereign People ,” it would be a mistake to give credit to one group for the success of an election. Rather, achieving a consequential majority in America requires coalition building – and maintenance.

SoRelle Wyckoff Gaynor does not work for, consult, own shares in or receive funding from any company or organization that would benefit from this article, and has disclosed no relevant affiliations beyond their academic appointment.

articles.title: Ballard Starter Line
articles.author: Martin Pagel
paras: At the Ballard Town Hall meeting Sound Transit made it clear that they do not want to make any major changes to the BLE plans to avoid starting all over with the EIS process. They did consider at some point starting with a connection between Ballard and Westlake and delay or even skip the second downtown tunnel (DSTT2). But that would require a separate operations and maintenance facility (OMF) at Interbay or connecting to the existing downtown tunnel (DSTT1). The tunnel is old and surrounding soil is unstable and therefore they concluded this would be very risky and costly. Tom Terrific however suggested a single-track maintenance tunnel connection which would connect at the end of the current tunnel by the Convention Center.

While any major design change (such as an elevated line) may jeopardize the current EIS process, implementing a project in phases is common and accepted. Not spending $8b on a second downtown tunnel at this point would allow Sound Transit to connect Ballard much earlier (in particular if paired with other measures such as automating the line or a ship canal gondola ). With all the downtown complexities it would also reduce a lot of risks. And as almost half of the tunnel is covered by funds collected in Pierce and Snohomish County and the Eastside, it may even allow Sound Transit to finish the spine earlier, a goal the Board keeps reiterating.

Sound Transit has also stated that the Ballard line is necessary to connect to the Tacoma line as an Everett to Tacoma line would get too long for operators, but they could turn Tacoma trains around at Northgate or just change operators halfway.

Sound Transit studied alternatives for a second tunnel. Either the line could connect to the existing tunnel (interlining) by tapping into the existing tunnel at Pine St and 3rd or operate as a separate line with a separate OMF at Interbay. They determined that both options would not be any cheaper than proceeding with a second tunnel. I tend to agree with the risks involved with tapping the existing tunnel for interlining. However, Tom’s suggestion for a single track to connect a Ballard line with the existing tunnel should warrant further research. To reduce operational impact, such track could be used during off-hours. It would allow maintaining trains at the SODO OMF instead of having to build a separate OMF.

Before the original tunnel was extended to Capitol Hill with a slight curve to the south, it used to have a track extending straight east of the Westlake station for trains to turn around. It might be possible to extend that tunnel portion and add a north turn. You may need to use the I-5 Express Lane exit to build such track. That track could then connect with the Ballard line roughly at the Denny station. It would be fairly long but for a maintenance track that should not matter as much.

Adding such a maintenance tunnel would be expensive, but not nearly as much as building a second tunnel or a separate Interbay OMF. I hope it would allow Sound Transit to serve Ballard well before 2042.

articles.title: 'The Forge District': Kirkland Gives NE 85th Station Area a Rebrand
articles.author: Ryan Packer
paras: The City of Kirkland is hoping a new name for the area around a forthcoming bus rapid transit station can aid in revitalization efforts, after years of lackluster development activity there. Last week, the Kirkland City Council picked "The Forge District" as its preferred moniker for the area after considering several other alternatives for a rebrand that is intended to foster a "distinct identity" and punch up marketing for potential developers.

NE 85th Street Station, situated in the median of I-405, will see double-decker express bus service starting in 2029 as part of the Sound Transit S2 line , and existing ST Express buses will stop at the interchange as soon as next year. But the development spark that city leaders have been hoping to see in the immediate area has not yet caught fire, despite a 2023 rezone that provided significant development capacity.

About a mile from the heart of Kirkland's charming downtown, the 710-acre station area stands at the confluence of several other neighborhoods including Rose Hill, Everest, and Norkirk. Though the vision is a "thriving, new walkable district with high tech and family wage jobs, plentiful affordable housing, sustainable buildings, park amenities, and commercial and retail services linked by transit," the area remains dominated by car dealerships, drive-through businesses today, and the freeway looming overhead.

Following the selection of a name, a visual branding scheme will follow, "to create collateral to support retention and recruitment of businesses, property owners, developers, and investors," according to a staff report provided to councilmembers.

"When we talk about the naming for NE 85th, it's not just for us as current community members or business owners, but it is also looking at those who will be coming here in the future," Jen Davis Hayes, Kirkland's Economic Development Manager, said ahead of the final naming vote.

Why the Forge? "Heat, energy," noted a presentation created by the consultant company Watson Creative. "Complimentary juxtaposition to softer Rose Hill, Norkirk, Juanita, Houghton, Totem Lake, Bridle Trails."
"Scales well: Forge Building, Forge Station, Forge Park."

The Forge District also references the steel foundry built by the city's namesake, Peter Kirk, in 1890. That steel mill "never produced a single ingot," according to the Kirkland Heritage Society , and its closure in the wake of the 1893 national economic crisis prompted Kirk to retire away from the city that still bears his name.

"Early on this process, we had thought about ways to sort of honor Indigenous names, and for many very good reasons, we moved away from that," Deputy Mayor Neal Black said during a discussion in September. "And I think once we've moved away from that, this way of honoring the history, the steel mill, it's meaningful to me, and I think it could be meaningful to a lot of longtime Kirklanders."

The runners-up were The Rise District and The Union District, with a last-minute entrant provided by the Kirkland Heritage Society: the Kellett District. It was John George Kellett, another British businessman seeking his fortune in a sparsely-populated Eastside in the late 19th Century, that decided to name a fledgling town after Kirk. Among other reasons, that name was discarded as being potentially tricky for newcomers to spell.

Though Kirkland is clearly taking the idea of a marketing campaign as a way to raise the area's profile seriously, the future of the neighborhood will almost certainly hinge more on economics. Earlier this year, the Kirkland Council gave the 85th Station area zoning code another tweak intended to spur development, extending a "pioneer provision" that gives the first developers prepared to break ground a discount on affordable housing requirements through 2030.

Those tweaks also included added flexibility when it comes to future development agreements, potentially setting the stage for larger buildings than might otherwise be allowed under code today. Also included were prohibitions on townhome development throughout most of the area, a move intended to prevent the area from getting locked in to an underbuilt form.

The Council also took the step earlier this year of fully removing requirements for off-street parking within the entire station area, going further than a new state mandate in the hopes of providing maximum flexibility for potential builders.
But if the area is primed for a future boom, it hasn't arrived yet.

"We know that these areas are well-suited to accommodate future population and employment growth, and they also represent priority areas for transportation funding, so with that in mind we've recently done a lot of work to update the zoning in the station area to support the transportation investments," Kirkland Senior Planner LeAndra Baker-Lewis told the city's planning commission this past spring. "But we haven't seen a notable amount of development that would help bolster those investments."

Though the 85th station area isn't currently the most accommodating place to get around by walking or biking, Kirkland has been endeavoring to make inroads on that front as well. Just this fall, the City opened a new multiuse path connecting Downtown Kirkland and the future bus station. However, that project comes after Kirkland spent $3.7 million to add a third vehicle lane to NE 85th Street around 120th Avenue NE.

Though construction is well underway on Sound Transit's $2.4 billion Stride BRT program, which will include three total lines from Burien to Lynnwood, interest from developers when it comes to creating transit-oriented development near those future stations has been tepid at best.

In Renton, a recent rezone has primed the area around a Stride station that will include connections to two separate RapidRide lines, but builders are not yet beating down Renton's door to get their projects permitted there – a fact that stands in contrast with development activity around the 2 Line in Bellevue .
But there's a chance new Eastside residents would rather live in The Forge than in a neighborhood called Wilburton.

"Once one of these names is chosen, it would be interesting to talk about signage," Kirkland Councilmember John Tymczyszyn said last month. "Being called the Forge District would be a lot more interesting, in my opinion, if there was 100-foot-high steel sign when you drive up 85th and into this district, so that the name kind of resonates with people that visit that area."

articles.title: Friday Roundtable: Historic Transit Investments in Puget Sound
articles.author: Michael Smith
paras: The past 5 days may have been the most consequential week for transit in Puget Sound this year. Across the region, voters and elected officials decided to invest in transit for years and decades to come.

On Tuesday, voters in Seattle approved the Seattle Transit Measure (STM) with an overwhelming 72% supporting the measure. The 0.3% sales tax increase will take effect on April 1, 2027 and fund 280,000 bus trips in Seattle each year for 10 years. The measure also funds 22,000 free ORCA cards for low-income, elderly, and families with young children, maintain support for Seattle’s streetcar lines, fund spot improvements to keep buses moving, and help expedite permits and inspections for Link expansion projects in Seattle. The additional bus trips will help grow Seattle’s Very Frequent Transit Network .

In Pierce County, 58% of voters approved a significant expansion to Pierce Transit on Tuesday. The approved proposition increases the sales and use tax within the Pierce County Public Transportation Benefit Area by 0.3%. With this additional funding, Piece Transit will add four new routes, upgrade existing routes 1, 2, and 3 to Stream lines, run most routes until 10pm (8pm on Sunday), and double weekend frequencies from 1hr to 30min on 15 routes. Pierce Transit will also add seasonal and special event service when needed and expand paratransit services. The additional funding will support free fares for seniors aged 65+. Free fares for seniors will start on April 1, 2027. The new routes and other changes will be rolled out in phases to allow time for planning, hiring additional staff, and buying new buses.

On Wednesday, the Everett City Council voted unanimously voted to approve the merger of Everett Transit and Community Transit. The Community Transit Board voted to approve the merger the following day. With these votes, Everett Transit end operations on March 31, 2027. Beginning April 1, Community Transit will operate all current Everett Transit routes and CT is required to maintain or exceed the existing level of service during the transition. Over the four years following the merger, Community Transit will increase service hours in Everett by 50%. In addition, CT will add a new Zip microtransit zone in Everett by March 2028.

To fund the additional service, Community Transit’s 1.2% sales tax will replace Everett’s existing 0.6% sales tax on April 1, 2027. Fares on existing Everett Transit routes will remain at $2 until at least April 2028. Any changes to the fares will require approval from the Community Transit Board.

Community Transit will pay Everett $54.5 million for the existing transit infrastructure and to mitigate any transition costs to the City. Separately, Everett will transfer $16 million in existing transit capital reserves to support replacing buses and other equipment.

Within the past week, voters in Seattle and Pierce County and elected officials in Snohomish County decided to invest in transit. The service improvements across the region will make traveling easier and more convenient for hundreds of thousands of people everyday. As Everett and Tacoma prepare for their respective Link extensions, the decisions made this week will ensure each Link extension connects with a robust bus network.

articles.title: Cafe Lolo Is the Neighborhood Restaurant Every Neighborhood Deserves
articles.author: <name>Kat Thompson</name>
paras: If I were to describe the perfect neighborhood restaurant, Cafe Lolo would completely fit my definition. The food is comforting and nourishing, emphasizing local ingredients, which playfully come together in a way that feels both fresh and familiar. The space is draped in natural light that’s assisted by over a dozen lamps. The inviting dining room is covered in quirky Renaissance-inspired murals that don’t feel disruptive. There are to-go meal kits available for purchase, as well as local beers. It’s an atmosphere that invites you to unwind with a bottle of wine. Owners Leah Engel, Alex Halmi, and Brett Bankson are present, not only flitting about the room, but also cooking the dishes in the kitchen and laughing with customers. If I lived in the neighborhood, just off the main drag of Capitol Hill, it’s somewhere I’d want to return to over and over again.

Cafe Lolo has an extensive wine menu and many local beers, as well as bottles in the fridge you can pick up to-go. Although yes, the wine list — which includes just one glass from Washington, and more options from Oregon and Europe) — is worth perusing, the nonalcoholic tisanes are also made from seasonal ingredients. The strawberry rhubarb soda I had on my visit was effervescent and floral without an overpowering sweetness.

Like the rest of the menu, dessert will change pending seasons — but don’t skip it. My visit included a celebration of ripe, macerated strawberries over a semolina olive oil cake, which had a buttery crust and a tender interior crumb. There was also a scoop of rhubarb sorbet; light, sweet, and sharp.

Boutiques and cocktail bars line Ballard Avenue (home to one of Seattle’s few year-round farmers markets ), and townhomes and high-rises have taken the place of single-family homes. Some of the best restaurants and bars in the city can be found here, along with almost (almost!) too many breweries , which is why if you walk far enough inland you can literally smell the hops.
